glyceryl-trinitrate.name: Glyceryl trinitrate
glyceryl-trinitrate.summary: A fast-acting nitrate spray or tablet under the tongue that widens veins and coronary arteries to relieve an angina attack within minutes.
usedFor: Relieving an angina attack within minutes (spray or tablet under the tongue)
Preventing angina before exertion
Intravenous infusion for unstable angina, heart attack with ongoing pain and acute heart failure
Long-acting isosorbide mononitrate for regular angina prevention; GTN ointment for anal fissures
glyceryl-trinitrate.howItWorks: Releases nitric oxide in vascular smooth muscle, activating guanylate cyclase and relaxing the vessel. Veins dilate most, so less blood returns to the heart and it has less to pump against (lower preload and wall tension, lower oxygen demand); coronary arteries and collaterals widen, improving supply to ischaemic muscle. Relief within minutes is typical of angina, but GTN also eases other pains and relief does not rule out a heart attack; pain that does not settle needs emergency help.

common: Throbbing headache (from dilated scalp vessels), flushing
Dizziness and faintness from a drop in blood pressure: sit down before using
serious: Severe hypotension and collapse if combined with sildenafil, tadalafil, vardenafil or similar drugs: nitrates and PDE-5 inhibitors are contraindicated together, and emergency staff need to know about any recent dose
Fast heart rate; rarely worsening of angina; methaemoglobinaemia with prolonged infusion

cautions: Tolerance develops with continuous exposure: long-acting nitrates need a nitrate-free interval each day
If pain persists 5 minutes after a second dose, call emergency services: it may be a heart attack
Severe aortic stenosis, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, very low blood pressure, raised intracranial pressure
Tablets lose potency after 8 weeks once opened; sprays last longer
glyceryl-trinitrate.monitoring: Blood pressure during infusions; frequency of spray use is a marker of angina control.

regulatory.note: Sublingual spray and tablets are pharmacy (P) medicines
Patches, buccal tablets and infusions

regimenNote: Sublingual spray 400 micrograms per dose or tablets; patches; intravenous infusion; modified-release tablets (isosorbide)

apixaban.name: Apixaban and DOACs
apixaban.summary: A direct oral anticoagulant that blocks clotting factor Xa, preventing strokes in atrial fibrillation and treating deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism without routine blood monitoring. It starts to work within hours, is taken twice a day with or without food, and its main harm is bleeding, so people carry an anticoagulant alert card and tell every dentist and surgeon they see.
usedFor: Preventing stroke in atrial fibrillation (first choice over warfarin for most)
Treating and preventing deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism
Preventing clots after hip and knee replacement
Not used for mechanical heart valves or antiphospholipid syndrome (warfarin remains)
apixaban.howItWorks: Binds directly to activated factor X, the enzyme at the junction of the clotting cascade that converts prothrombin to thrombin. Less thrombin means less fibrin, so clots that form in the slow-flowing left atrial appendage or leg veins are prevented or stopped from growing. Unlike warfarin the effect is predictable, starts within hours, needs no blood-level monitoring and is little affected by diet. The NHS describes the same action in plain terms: apixaban stops a clotting factor called factor Xa from working, which makes the blood take longer to clot. That is also why its harms are the mirror image of its benefit: cuts bleed for longer, bruises appear more easily and fade more slowly, and bleeding inside the body, including into the brain, is the serious risk. Because the effect fades within a day or so of the last dose, protection depends on taking it consistently; the US product information carries a boxed warning that people with atrial fibrillation who stop apixaban face a higher risk of stroke, so a doctor who needs to stop it usually arranges another anticoagulant to cover the gap.
apixaban.onset: Peak effect 3-4 hours after a dose; the NHS notes it starts working within a few hours of the first dose. Wears off within a day or two of stopping, which is why missed doses matter and why stopping is never done without medical advice.

common: Bleeding more easily: bleeding for longer than usual from cuts, nosebleeds, bleeding gums when brushing, bruises that come up more easily and take longer to fade, heavier and longer periods
Anaemia, which can cause tiredness and paler skin
Nausea, rash
serious: Major bleeding: gastrointestinal (blood in the stool, red or black tarry stools, blood in vomit), urinary (pink, brown or red urine), coughing up blood, intracranial (about half the rate of warfarin; a sudden severe headache with confusion, sensitivity to light or slurred speech), retroperitoneal

Bleeding after trauma or surgery: a fall or injury on apixaban, especially a blow to the head, needs urgent assessment even without visible bleeding; reversal agents (andexanet, idarucizumab for dabigatran) exist but are limited

Spinal haematoma with epidural or spinal anaesthesia or spinal injection, which can cause paralysis: weakness or numbness of the legs or feet, or loss of bladder or bowel control afterwards, is an emergency
Ongoing bleeding that does not stop on its own

cautions: Dose reduced with kidney impairment, low weight, age over 80 (apixaban), and some interacting drugs

Avoid NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen) and aspirin unless specifically advised, and check before starting herbal products, which can also interact; alcohol in moderation, because heavy or binge drinking increases the effect of apixaban and the risk of bleeding

Before surgery or procedures the clinical team decides whether to pause apixaban and for how long, depending on bleeding risk and kidney function; it is not stopped unless the clinician says so; the anticoagulant alert card is shown to doctors and dentists before any surgery or dental treatment
Missed doses matter because the effect wears off quickly; do not double up. Treatment is not stopped without medical advice because the clot or stroke risk returns as the drug wears off
apixaban.monitoring: Kidney function, blood count and weight at least yearly (more often if kidney function is poor); no INR needed. Monitoring is otherwise clinical: looking for bruising, bleeding, anaemia symptoms and checking that doses are not being missed.

sections.heading: What is apixaban used for?
sections.body:
Apixaban is an anticoagulant, a medicine that helps prevent blood clots from forming. It is available in the UK only on prescription.

The NHS says it is used to treat blood clots in the veins, such as deep vein thrombosis (DVT), and in the lungs, called pulmonary embolism. It is also given to people at high risk of clots, such as those with atrial fibrillation (an irregular heartbeat), heart failure, or a past stroke or transient ischaemic attack (TIA). It is also given after a recent hip or knee replacement.

sections.heading: How does apixaban work and how is it taken?
sections.body:
Apixaban makes the blood take longer to clot, which lowers the chance of a harmful clot but also means bleeding can last longer. The tablets can be taken with or without food.

The NHS says a person should not stop apixaban without talking to their doctor. If it is stopped, the way the blood clots goes back to what it was before treatment, usually within a day or two. The NHS gives missed-dose advice on its anticoagulant dosage page; it depends on how long it is until the next scheduled dose.

sections.heading: What are the side effects of apixaban?
sections.body:
The most common side effect is bleeding more easily than normal. This can show as nosebleeds, bleeding gums, bruising or heavier periods. The NHS describes this kind of bleeding as not dangerous, and says it should stop by itself. The doctor should be told if it bothers the person or does not stop.

The NHS lists blood in urine or stools, and coughing up or vomiting blood, among the more serious effects. On its main apixaban page, the NHS says to call NHS 111 for symptoms of bleeding, a head injury, or other possible serious side effects.

Very rarely, apixaban can cause bleeding in the brain. On its side-effects page the NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E for a sudden severe headache unlike any before, fits, sudden loss of vision or blurred vision, or numbness or tingling in the arms or legs. The two NHS pages are worded differently: the main page names NHS 111 for bleeding and head injury, and the side-effects page names 999 or A&E for these brain-bleed signs.

A serious allergic reaction, such as swelling of the face or throat or difficulty breathing, is a reason to call 999.

sections.heading: Can I take other medicines or drink alcohol with apixaban?
sections.body:
The NHS says some medicines may not mix well with apixaban, including other anticoagulants, some antidepressants, and painkillers or anti-inflammatories such as aspirin and ibuprofen. The NHS says not to take aspirin or ibuprofen unless a doctor has said it is fine, as they raise the chance of bleeding.

The NHS asks people to tell their doctor, dentist or pharmacist about every medicine they take, including over-the-counter medicines, vitamins and herbal supplements. It names St John's wort, a herbal remedy for low mood, as one to avoid. It also says there is not enough information to say that other herbal remedies and supplements are safe to take with apixaban.

The NHS says it is possible to drink alcohol while taking apixaban, but heavy or binge drinking raises the risk of bleeding.

sections.heading: Apixaban, surgery and the alert card
sections.body: The NHS says people taking apixaban should carry an anticoagulant alert card and tell their surgeon or dentist that they take it. Because of the risk of bleeding, the dose may need to be lowered or stopped a few days before an operation, and the clinical team makes that decision.

sections.heading: Who may not be able to take apixaban?
sections.body:
The NHS lists reasons apixaban may not be suitable, including a past allergic reaction to apixaban or any other medicine, active heavy bleeding, a stomach ulcer, a recent bleed in the brain, and liver or kidney problems.

The NHS says apixaban can be harmful to a baby, so pregnancy or trying to become pregnant is on its list of reasons. It also says apixaban should not be used while breastfeeding.

faqs.q: Is apixaban an anticoagulant?
faqs.a: Yes. The NHS describes apixaban as an anticoagulant that helps prevent blood clots. It is only available on prescription in the UK.

faqs.q: What does the NHS say about a missed apixaban tablet?
faqs.a: The NHS gives missed-dose advice on its anticoagulant dosage page. It depends on how long it is until the next scheduled dose, and this site does not give the timings.

faqs.q: Can apixaban be stopped if someone feels fine?
faqs.a: The NHS says not to stop apixaban without talking to the doctor first. If it is stopped, the way the blood clots returns to what it was before treatment, usually within a day or two.

faqs.q: What does the NHS say about a head injury or bleeding on apixaban?
faqs.a: On its main apixaban page, the NHS says to call NHS 111 for symptoms of bleeding, a head injury or other possible serious side effects. On its side-effects page, it says to call 999 or go to A&E for a sudden severe headache, fits, or sudden vision changes.

faqs.q: Can alcohol be drunk while taking apixaban?
faqs.a: The NHS says it is possible to drink alcohol while taking apixaban. Heavy or binge drinking raises the risk of bleeding.

warfarin.name: Warfarin
warfarin.summary: The long-established oral anticoagulant that blocks vitamin K-dependent clotting factors; effective for mechanical heart valves and clots but needs regular INR blood tests and careful dosing. Its main serious harm is bleeding, which US labelling carries as a boxed warning, and because the dose each person needs varies with diet, illness, alcohol and a very long list of interacting medicines, treatment is organised around the INR test, an anticoagulant alert card and a steady routine rather than around a fixed dose.
usedFor: Mechanical heart valves (the only oral anticoagulant licensed)
Atrial fibrillation with moderate or severe mitral stenosis, and antiphospholipid syndrome
Venous thromboembolism where DOACs are unsuitable (severe kidney failure, cost)

Historically the standard anticoagulant, now largely replaced by DOACs for other indications; US information lists prevention and treatment of blood clots and prevention of complications in people with certain irregular heart rhythms, mechanical valves or a previous heart attack or stroke
warfarin.howItWorks: Blocks vitamin K epoxide reductase in the liver, so vitamin K cannot be recycled to activate clotting factors II, VII, IX and X. Existing factors take days to be cleared, so the effect starts after 2-3 days and heparin cover is needed for immediate protection. The dose needed varies enormously between people and with diet, illness and other drugs, so the INR blood test tunes it. StatPearls summarises the action as blocking the production of the vitamin K-dependent clotting factors, which lowers the blood's ability to clot, and describes warfarin as a narrow-therapeutic-index drug: the gap between too little effect (clots) and too much (bleeding) is small, which is why it is subject to so many clinically important interactions and why close INR monitoring is regarded as essential. The dependence on vitamin K explains the dietary advice: vitamin K-rich foods such as leafy green vegetables, chickpeas and liver push the INR down, so the NHS advises keeping intake consistent rather than avoiding these foods, while cranberry juice and grapefruit juice increase the blood-thinning effect and are avoided. The effect also outlasts the last dose by several days, so stopping or interrupting warfarin before operations and dental extractions is planned by the clinic, never by the person alone. The same mechanism is used against rodents: warfarin was first marketed as a rodenticide, and the far more potent 'superwarfarin' pesticides cause prolonged anticoagulation when ingested. A rare inherited warfarin resistance means some people need unusually high doses to reach the same effect.
warfarin.onset: Therapeutic after 3-5 days; effect persists 3-5 days after stopping. Reversed with vitamin K (slow) or prothrombin complex concentrate (immediate). Because the effect lingers for days, stopping is never done without the anticoagulant clinic's advice.

common: Bruising, bleeding gums, nosebleeds: the NHS lists unexplained bruising and nosebleeds among the signs of bleeding to report
Hair thinning, rash
Heavier menstrual bleeding
serious: Major bleeding, including intracranial: risk rises steeply when the INR is above 4. Warning signs are blood in the urine or stools, coughing up or vomiting blood, and a sudden severe headache with confusion or weakness, which can mean bleeding in the brain; any head injury on warfarin needs urgent assessment (NHS 111) even without visible bleeding

US labelling carries a boxed warning that warfarin can cause serious, sometimes fatal bleeding, more likely in older people, at higher doses and with long-term use; newer DOACs cause about half as many bleeds into the brain as warfarin
Skin necrosis in the first days (protein C deficiency), purple toe syndrome; a painful skin rash can also signal calciphylaxis, a rare condition in which small blood vessels calcify

Fetal harm: teratogenic in the first trimester and bleeding later; StatPearls notes it is generally avoided in pregnancy but considered in selected high-risk situations such as mechanical heart valves, and that it is compatible with breastfeeding because little passes into milk
Serious allergic reaction (anaphylaxis), rare

cautions: Hundreds of interactions: antibiotics, antifungals, amiodarone, NSAIDs, alcohol binges raise the INR; rifampicin, carbamazepine, large amounts of green vegetables lower it. The NHS names NSAIDs such as ibuprofen, aspirin, antibiotics and antidepressants among common interacting medicines, and US information adds herbal products; every new medicine or supplement is checked first

Keep vitamin K intake steady rather than avoiding it (leafy greens, chickpeas, liver); cranberry juice and grapefruit juice are avoided because they increase the effect; alcohol is kept within modest daily limits and binge drinking avoided

Carry an anticoagulant alert card; tell dentists and pharmacists. The card is shown before any operation, dental work (especially extractions), tattoo or piercing, because the clinic may need to lower or pause the dose beforehand; vaccinations are usually fine but staff are told
Target INR 2-3 for most indications, 2.5-3.5 for some mechanical valves

Unsuitable or used with great care in people with liver or kidney problems, uncontrolled high blood pressure, a recent stroke, recent or imminent surgery, pregnancy, or conditions that make bleeding more likely such as a stomach ulcer
Missed or extra doses are reported to the anticoagulant clinic, GP or NHS 111 rather than corrected by the person
Switching between warfarin and a DOAC is managed by the clinic, with an INR test used to time the change
warfarin.monitoring: INR every few days at first, then every 4-12 weeks once stable, and after any new drug or illness; self-testing meters are available. The NHS describes the INR being checked often, sometimes every other day, until the dose is right and less frequently once stable, with the dose adjusted by the clinic until the INR sits in the target range; home INR meters can be used after training but are usually bought privately. Between tests people are told to report bleeding, head injuries and new medicines straight away. Under-anticoagulation leaves the person exposed to clots and over-anticoagulation to bleeding, so both directions matter.

sections.heading: What is warfarin used for, and how is it monitored?
sections.body:
Warfarin is an anticoagulant, often called a blood thinner, used to prevent and treat blood clots. It does not literally thin the blood; it makes clots form less readily. Because it lowers the chance of clots, the main risk that comes with it is bleeding.

People taking warfarin are given an anticoagulant alert card. Regular blood tests measure how quickly the blood clots, and the result guides the warfarin dose. This test is called the international normalised ratio, or INR. Testing is usually more frequent while the right dose is being found.

sections.heading: What are the side effects of warfarin?
sections.body:
The main side effect of warfarin is an increased risk of bleeding. The NHS lists blood in the urine or poo, unexplained bruising or nosebleeds, and coughing up or vomiting blood among the signs of bleeding.

The NHS says to get urgent advice from NHS 111 if there are signs of bleeding, after a head injury, or if another serious side effect is suspected. Severe bleeding that will not stop needs a 999 call or A&E. A sudden bad headache with confusion, slurred speech or difficulty moving the arms or legs can signal bleeding in the brain, which is an emergency needing a 999 call.

A painful skin rash can be a sign of a rare condition called calciphylaxis. A severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) is an emergency needing a 999 call. Both are listed on the NHS page.

sections.heading: Can I eat and drink what I like on warfarin?
sections.body:
Foods rich in vitamin K, such as leafy greens, affect how warfarin works. The NHS says they can still be eaten; keeping the amount steady matters more than avoiding them, and the warfarin clinic can adjust the dose to match. Cranberry juice and grapefruit juice are best avoided because they can increase the blood-thinning effect.

The NHS advises never binge drinking on warfarin, and keeping regular drinking modest.

sections.heading: Can I take other medicines, supplements or herbal remedies with warfarin?
sections.body: The NHS says some medicines, remedies and supplements may not mix well with warfarin, so a doctor should know about everything else a person takes. Painkillers such as ibuprofen, antibiotics, antidepressants and statins are among the medicines the NHS lists as possible problems. The NHS advises against St John's wort and vitamin K supplements while on warfarin. Illness with sickness or diarrhoea can change how warfarin works, so the anticoagulant clinic is told about illness as well as new medicines.

sections.heading: Who needs extra care with warfarin, and what about pregnancy?
sections.body:
The NHS says most people can take warfarin, but it is not suitable for everyone. It lists an allergy to warfarin, liver or kidney problems, a recent stroke, recent or planned surgery, and a condition that makes bleeding more likely.

Warfarin is not usually used in pregnancy because it can affect the baby's development, though it is sometimes used after the doctor discusses risks and benefits. The NHS advises anyone who is pregnant or planning a pregnancy to speak to their GP or anticoagulant clinic, and not to stop warfarin unless a doctor says so. The NHS says warfarin can usually be taken while breastfeeding, after discussing it with a GP or midwife first.

faqs.q: Does warfarin really thin the blood?
faqs.a: Not literally; it is called a blood thinner, but it makes clots form less readily. The NHS describes it as a medicine used to prevent and treat blood clots, and says its main side effect is an increased risk of bleeding.

faqs.q: What is an anticoagulant alert card?
faqs.a: It is a card given to people taking warfarin, who may be at risk of bleeding.

faqs.q: What should be done after a head injury on warfarin?
faqs.a: The NHS says to get urgent advice from NHS 111 after a head injury while on warfarin, as well as for any signs of bleeding. A sudden bad headache with confusion, slurred speech or difficulty moving the arms or legs can signal bleeding in the brain and needs a 999 call.

faqs.q: Do I have to avoid green vegetables on warfarin?
faqs.a: No. Leafy greens are rich in vitamin K and affect warfarin, but the NHS says they can still be eaten and that a steady intake matters, so the clinic can adjust the dose. Cranberry juice and grapefruit juice are the drinks to avoid.

faqs.q: Can warfarin be taken in pregnancy?
faqs.a: The NHS says warfarin is not usually used in pregnancy because it can affect the baby's development, although it is sometimes used after the doctor talks through risks and benefits. Anyone pregnant or planning a pregnancy is advised to speak to their GP or anticoagulant clinic and not to stop it unless a doctor says so.

metformin.name: Metformin
metformin.summary: The first-line tablet for type 2 diabetes: it reduces the glucose the liver releases and improves the body's response to insulin, without causing low blood sugar on its own.
usedFor: First-line drug for type 2 diabetes alongside diet and exercise
Prediabetes in people at high risk
Polycystic ovary syndrome (off label) and gestational diabetes
metformin.howItWorks: Reduces the amount of glucose the liver releases into blood (by inhibiting gluconeogenesis via AMP-activated protein kinase and the mitochondrial redox state), increases the sensitivity of muscle and fat to insulin, and modestly reduces glucose absorption from the gut. It does not stimulate insulin release, so it does not cause hypoglycaemia on its own or weight gain; HbA1c falls by about 11 mmol/mol (1%).
metformin.onset: Glucose lowering within days; full effect in 2-3 weeks. Started low and increased weekly.

common: Nausea, diarrhoea, bloating, metallic taste (a third at the start, most settle; take with food, build up slowly, or use modified release)
Vitamin B12 deficiency with long-term use
serious: Lactic acidosis: very rare, but dangerous when the drug accumulates in kidney failure, or in severe illness, dehydration, sepsis, heart failure or heavy alcohol use
Hypoglycaemia only when combined with insulin or sulfonylureas

cautions: Dose reduced when eGFR is below 45 and stopped below 30
Pause during acute illness with dehydration ('sick day rules') and around iodine contrast scans and surgery
Check B12 if anaemia, tingling or fatigue develop
Alcohol in moderation
metformin.monitoring: HbA1c every 3-6 months; kidney function at least yearly; B12 periodically.

metformin.understand: Metformin lowers blood glucose mainly by telling the liver to release less sugar between meals, and by helping muscle respond to insulin. It does not make the pancreas release more insulin, so on its own it does not cause low blood sugar.
metformin.mechanismDetail: Metformin accumulates in hepatocytes via the OCT1 transporter and reduces hepatic gluconeogenesis: it lowers the mitochondrial energy state (partial inhibition of complex I and of mitochondrial glycerophosphate dehydrogenase, shifting the cytosolic redox state) and activates AMP-activated protein kinase, which suppresses gluconeogenic gene expression and lipogenesis. Peripheral insulin sensitivity improves modestly, intestinal glucose uptake and GLP-1 secretion increase, and the gut microbiome changes. Because insulin secretion is not stimulated, hypoglycaemia does not occur with monotherapy and weight is neutral or slightly reduced. Metformin is not metabolised and is cleared by the kidney (tubular secretion); accumulation in renal failure, hypoxia or severe illness impairs lactate clearance and can precipitate lactic acidosis. It reduces ileal vitamin B12 absorption.

Iodinated contrast media: metformin is withheld on the day of a contrast procedure and for 48 hours afterwards in people with reduced kidney function, and restarted once kidney function is confirmed stable.
Sick-day guidance: during vomiting, diarrhoea, fever or any illness that stops eating and drinking, UK information advises pausing metformin and restarting 24-48 hours after recovery.

sections.heading: What is metformin used for and how does it work?
sections.body:
Metformin is a medicine that is used to treat type 2 diabetes. The NHS says it can also be used for gestational diabetes and for polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS), the name the NHS now uses for what was previously called polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). It is also used to help prevent type 2 diabetes in people at high risk of developing it. Gestational diabetes is diabetes that first appears during pregnancy.

The NHS says metformin lowers blood sugar levels by improving the way the body handles insulin. Other descriptions add that it reduces how much glucose the liver releases. For PMOS, the NHS says it works by lowering insulin and blood sugar levels, and that it can improve ovulation and encourage regular periods, even in people without diabetes. The NHS says this use is not officially approved. It comes as standard tablets, which release metformin quickly, and as slow-release tablets, which work gradually.

sections.heading: What are the side effects of metformin?
sections.body:
The NHS lists feeling or being sick, diarrhoea, tummy pain and loss of appetite among the common side effects. A change in taste is also listed. The NHS says most of these ease after a couple of weeks. The NHS advises taking metformin with a meal to reduce side effects. Vitamin B12 deficiency is also listed as a side effect and is more likely with long-term use. Doctors may check vitamin B12 levels with a blood test in some people who take metformin for a long time.

Lactic acidosis, a build-up of acid in the blood, is a very rare but serious side effect. Symptoms the NHS lists include being sick, stomach pain, muscle cramps, breathing problems and severe tiredness. The NHS says to call 999 if lactic acidosis or a severe allergic reaction is suspected. For other serious side effects, such as inflammation of the liver, the NHS says to call NHS 111. A UK patient leaflet says lactic acidosis can lead to serious illness that needs hospital care.

sections.heading: Taking metformin with alcohol, other illnesses or before scans
sections.body:
The NHS advises limiting how much alcohol is drunk while taking metformin, because it can increase the risk of serious side effects. UK leaflets say drinking too much alcohol may increase the risk of lactic acidosis.

A UK patient leaflet says metformin is stopped before or at the time of an injection of contrast dye, and the doctor says when to restart. A review of manufacturers' labels found that all of them advise stopping metformin before scans that use contrast dye. UK patient leaflets say metformin is stopped for a short time with a condition that may cause dehydration, such as severe vomiting or diarrhoea. The NHS says that anyone who has taken more than the prescribed amount should call NHS 111.

sections.heading: Who needs extra care with metformin?
sections.body:
The NHS says most adults and children aged 10 years and over can take metformin, but some people should tell the doctor first. These include people with uncontrolled diabetes, liver or kidney problems, a severe infection, heart failure or a high alcohol intake. A past allergic reaction to metformin is also on the NHS list.

The risk of lactic acidosis is higher when the kidneys do not work well, UK patient leaflets say. The same leaflets say the doctor checks how well the kidneys work regularly during treatment. The NHS says that if blood sugar levels are stable, metformin should not affect the ability to drive, cycle or use machinery and tools. The NHS says the risk comes from other diabetes medicines that can lower blood sugar.

sections.heading: Metformin in pregnancy and breastfeeding
sections.body:
The NHS says metformin can be taken in pregnancy, but advises checking with a doctor first. The NHS says that in gestational diabetes, medicines taken to control blood sugar are usually stopped after the baby is born.

The NHS says that if the doctor or midwife says the baby is healthy, metformin can be taken while breastfeeding. Only tiny amounts pass into breast milk, the NHS says. A review of manufacturers' labels found that they advise against metformin during breastfeeding, which differs from the NHS advice. The NHS says a health professional should be contacted if a breastfed baby feeds poorly or seems unusually drowsy or restless. The NHS also says that if metformin causes vomiting or severe diarrhoea for more than 24 hours, contraceptive pills may not protect against pregnancy.

faqs.q: Can metformin cause lactic acidosis?
faqs.a: Lactic acidosis is a very rare but serious side effect. The NHS lists being sick, stomach pain, muscle cramps, breathing problems and severe tiredness as symptoms. It says to call 999 if lactic acidosis is suspected. UK patient leaflets say the risk is higher when the kidneys do not work well, and that heavy drinking may also raise it.

faqs.q: How can the stomach side effects of metformin be eased?
faqs.a: The NHS says the most common side effects are feeling or being sick, diarrhoea, tummy pain and loss of appetite. It advises taking metformin with a meal to reduce them, and says most side effects ease after a couple of weeks. Standard tablets release metformin quickly, while slow-release tablets work gradually.

faqs.q: Can alcohol be drunk while taking metformin?
faqs.a: The NHS advises limiting how much alcohol is drunk while taking metformin, because it can increase the risk of serious side effects. UK leaflets link drinking too much alcohol to a higher risk of lactic acidosis. The NHS asks people who drink heavily to tell the doctor before starting the medicine.

faqs.q: Can metformin cause vitamin B12 deficiency?
faqs.a: The NHS lists vitamin B12 deficiency among the side effects of metformin, and it is more likely with long-term use. Because of this, doctors may check vitamin B12 levels with a blood test in some people who take metformin for a long time. The common stomach side effects are separate, and most of them ease after a couple of weeks, the NHS says.

insulin.name: Insulin
insulin.summary: The hormone that moves glucose from the blood into cells, given by injection or pump to everyone with type 1 diabetes and to many with type 2 when other treatments are not enough. Preparations differ mainly in how quickly they start and how long they last, and are combined to copy the body's own pattern of a steady background supply plus bursts at meals; the price of that control is hypoglycaemia, the one side effect every insulin user learns to recognise and treat.
usedFor: Type 1 diabetes: essential for life from diagnosis, usually as a long-acting insulin once or twice a day plus a rapid-acting insulin before meals (a basal-bolus regimen), or rapid-acting insulin alone through a pump

Type 2 diabetes when tablets no longer control glucose, in pregnancy, and during severe illness or surgery; regimens include intermediate-acting insulin once or twice daily, a long-acting insulin, or a mixed (biphasic) insulin before meals
Diabetic ketoacidosis and hyperosmolar states (intravenous infusion)
Lowering dangerously high potassium (with glucose) in emergencies
Longer term, good glucose control with insulin lowers the risk of heart attack, stroke and the kidney, nerve, eye and gum complications of diabetes
insulin.howItWorks: Replaces the hormone the pancreatic beta cells no longer make. Insulin binds receptors on muscle, fat and liver cells, moving GLUT4 transporters to the surface so glucose enters cells; it switches the liver from making glucose to storing glycogen, stops fat breakdown and ketone production, and promotes protein synthesis. Modern analogue insulins are engineered to act fast at meals (aspart, lispro) or flat and long as background (glargine, degludec), mimicking the natural pattern of a basal trickle plus mealtime bursts. The NHS groups preparations into five families by their time course: rapid-acting analogues (aspart, lispro, glulisine), short-acting soluble human insulin, intermediate-acting isophane (NPH) insulin, long-acting analogues (detemir, glargine, degludec) and biphasic mixtures that blend an intermediate insulin with a rapid- or short-acting one. Among the long-acting insulins, detemir is usually given twice a day whereas glargine and degludec are usually given once, and degludec is often chosen for people troubled by night-time hypoglycaemia; analogues may act more consistently than older human insulins for some people. Insulin is a protein, so it is destroyed by digestion and must be injected under the skin or infused into a vein; an inhaled insulin exists in some countries but can reduce lung function and is avoided in asthma and COPD. The prescriber chooses the types, dose and timing, and most people with type 1 diabetes use more than one type.
insulin.onset: Rapid-acting 10-20 minutes (peak 1-3 hours, lasts 3-5 hours); long-acting flat over 24 hours or more. A long-acting dose taken later than usual keeps working later than usual, which raises the risk of a hypo and is why timing is kept consistent.

common: Hypoglycaemia (sweating, trembling or shaking, a fast heartbeat, tingling lips, dizziness, hunger, unusually pale skin, and with longer-acting insulins anxiety, confusion, difficulty concentrating or blurred vision): treat with 15-20 g fast sugar such as fruit juice, a sugary drink, glucose tablets, jelly babies or glucose gel, recheck, then a starchy snack because the sugar wears off quickly
Hypos are provoked by too much insulin, a missed or delayed meal, too little carbohydrate, and alcohol, especially on an empty stomach
Weight gain
Lipohypertrophy (fatty lumps) at over-used injection sites, which absorb insulin erratically
Bruising, bleeding, stinging, itching or redness at the injection site
serious: Severe hypoglycaemia with seizure or coma, needing glucagon injection or intravenous glucose; the NHS advises calling 999 if the person is not responding normally or is unconscious and glucagon is not available, if they have not recovered soon after glucagon, or if alcohol is involved
Diabetic ketoacidosis if insulin is omitted in type 1 diabetes (never stop, even when not eating: adjust instead)
Hypokalaemia with intravenous infusion
Allergy, including anaphylaxis (very rare with modern insulins): skin, lips or tongue turning blue, grey or pale, sudden confusion or fainting

cautions: Doses are individual and adjusted for food, activity, illness and glucose readings; errors in units are a major cause of harm ('units' written in full). Brands are not interchangeable, because some are more concentrated than others
Sick-day rules: keep taking basal insulin, check glucose and ketones more often, drink fluids
Driving rules: check glucose before and every 2 hours; carry fast sugar
Store unopened insulin in the fridge; in use at room temperature for 4 weeks
Rotate injection sites to avoid lipohypertrophy, which makes absorption erratic; frequent hypos, particularly at night, prompt a review of the regimen rather than simply eating more
Some products are withdrawn or discontinued from time to time (the NHS flags Levemir), so people are switched under supervision rather than left without a basal insulin
insulin.monitoring: Fingerprick or continuous glucose monitoring several times daily; HbA1c every 3-6 months; annual eye, foot and kidney checks. Monitoring is the basis of dose adjustment as advised by the diabetes team, and the NHS emphasises regular checking as the main way of preventing hypos; injection sites are inspected for lipohypertrophy at review.

levothyroxine.name: Levothyroxine
levothyroxine.summary: Synthetic thyroid hormone (T4) that replaces what an underactive thyroid cannot make, restoring energy, weight and metabolism; the dose is set by regular TSH blood tests. Because it stands in for a hormone the body is missing rather than adding a foreign drug action, side effects are uncommon at the right dose and most of those that occur are the signs of too much thyroid hormone; treatment is usually lifelong and the tablet is taken on an empty stomach, apart from the foods, supplements and medicines that stop it being absorbed.
usedFor: Hypothyroidism from any cause (autoimmune, after surgery or radioiodine, congenital); it controls the condition rather than curing it, so it is continued even when the person feels well
Suppressing TSH after thyroid cancer, alongside surgery and radioactive iodine treatment
Subclinical hypothyroidism when TSH is high, symptomatic, or in pregnancy
Not used for weight loss in people whose thyroid works normally: US patient information warns that large doses, especially with amphetamines, can cause serious or life-threatening harm
levothyroxine.howItWorks: A synthetic copy of thyroxine (T4), the hormone the thyroid normally releases. Tissues convert it to the active T3, which enters cell nuclei and switches on genes controlling metabolic rate, heat production, heart rate, gut motility, growth and brain development. Replacement restores the pituitary's TSH to normal, which is how the dose is tuned. The NHS puts the same idea simply: levothyroxine is a synthetic version of T4, the main hormone the thyroid makes, and the body converts it into the more active T3, so it stands in for what an underactive gland is not producing. Because it replaces a hormone the body is missing, it usually has few effects of its own; what the person notices depends on whether the dose matches their need. Too little leaves the symptoms of hypothyroidism (tiredness, weight gain, feeling cold) in place, and too much produces the opposite picture of an overactive thyroid. The response is slow: some people feel better within days, others take several months, and the TSH result used to judge the dose takes weeks to settle after each change. Absorption from the gut is the weak point. The tablet is swallowed with water on an empty stomach and food is delayed afterwards, because food, coffee, calcium and iron supplements, antacids and foods such as soya, walnuts and high-fibre meals all reduce how much is taken up, which is why a missed dose or a dose taken too close to food can push the TSH up at the next test.
levothyroxine.onset: Symptoms improve over weeks; TSH takes 6-8 weeks to settle after each dose change. Lifelong. The NHS notes that some people feel better within days of starting while others take several months, and US information that several weeks may pass before any change in symptoms is noticed.

common: Few at the right dose; at too high a dose: palpitations, weight loss, sweating, anxiety, insomnia, diarrhoea (symptoms of hyperthyroidism). The NHS lists difficulty sleeping, headaches, feeling anxious, sweating and hair loss as the common effects and notes that they usually ease once the dose is adjusted
Temporary hair loss in the first months
US information also lists weight change, headache, vomiting, diarrhoea, changes in appetite and fever as less serious effects to mention to a doctor if they persist
serious: Angina or atrial fibrillation if started too fast in the elderly or those with heart disease (start at 25 micrograms); a racing heartbeat or chest pain after a dose is a reason to contact a doctor
Bone loss and atrial fibrillation with long-term over-replacement
Adrenal crisis if given before untreated adrenal insufficiency is corrected; people with adrenal gland conditions, heart disease, diabetes or an overactive thyroid are assessed before starting

Thyroid crisis from a sudden excess of hormone (rare): fever, a fast or irregular heartbeat, dizziness or fainting, or yellowing of the skin or eyes, which the NHS advises reporting urgently (NHS 111)
Serious allergic reaction (rare): swelling of the throat or tongue, an itchy raised rash or difficulty breathing needs emergency help

cautions: Absorption falls with calcium, iron, antacids, proton pump inhibitors, soya and coffee: separate by 4 hours. US information adds walnuts and high-fibre foods to the list of foods that can change how well the medicine works
Dose often needs to rise in pregnancy (increase by 25-50% and check TSH promptly), and with oestrogen, enzyme inducers
Stay on the same brand where possible: US information notes that different brands contain slightly different amounts of hormone, so a switch is not made without the prescriber or pharmacist knowing
Do not use for weight loss in people with normal thyroid function
Taken once a day on an empty stomach with a full glass of water, waiting before breakfast and caffeinated drinks; the tablet can stick in the throat if swallowed dry

Blood tests are timed in relation to the morning dose, and a missed dose or one taken with food can raise the TSH at the next test; extra doses taken by accident, a racing heart or chest pain are reported to a doctor
Breastfeeding is usually compatible, confirmed with a pharmacist or doctor; the dose is not stopped or changed without advice, since the body has no other source of the hormone
levothyroxine.monitoring: TSH 6-8 weeks after starting or changing dose, then yearly once stable. The NHS describes regular blood tests as the way the dose is confirmed: a follow-up test some weeks after every change, then a yearly check once the result is steady. Between tests the review is clinical, asking about symptoms of under- or over-replacement (tiredness and weight gain on one side; palpitations, sweating, anxiety, poor sleep and weight loss on the other) and checking for new medicines or supplements that interfere with absorption.

sections.heading: What is levothyroxine used for?
sections.body:
Levothyroxine is a medicine for an underactive thyroid, which is called hypothyroidism. The NHS says it suits most adults and children, though it is not right for everyone, so a clinician checks first.

MedlinePlus, a US source, says it is also used alongside surgery and radioactive iodine treatment for thyroid cancer. It warns that levothyroxine should not be used to lose weight, and that large amounts, especially with amphetamines, can cause serious or life-threatening harm.

sections.heading: How does levothyroxine work, and how long is it taken for?
sections.body:
Levothyroxine is a man-made version of thyroxine, the main hormone the thyroid makes, so it stands in for what an underactive gland is not producing. The NHS says treatment usually carries on for the rest of a person's life. MedlinePlus says people are told to keep taking it even when they feel well, and not to stop without talking to their doctor.

At first there are regular blood tests until the right amount is reached. Once the result is steady, the NHS says a blood test about once a year is usual.

sections.heading: What are the side effects of levothyroxine?
sections.body:
The NHS lists difficulty sleeping, headaches, feeling anxious, sweating and hair loss as the common side effects. It says most side effects happen when the dose is too high, and NHS leaflets describe signs of too much thyroid hormone such as sweating, headaches, diarrhoea and being sick.

Serious side effects are rare. The NHS lists a sudden rise in thyroid hormone, called thyroid crisis, which can cause a high temperature, a fast or irregular heartbeat, dizziness or faintness, and yellowing of the skin or eyes. It also lists a serious allergic reaction (anaphylaxis), with swelling of the throat or tongue, a raised itchy rash or difficulty breathing. For a suspected anaphylactic reaction the NHS says to call 999.

sections.heading: Can levothyroxine be taken with food, drinks or other medicines?
sections.body:
The NHS says levothyroxine is usually taken on an empty stomach, before the first meal of the day, and before any drink with caffeine, such as tea or coffee, or any other medicine. An NHS trust leaflet explains that caffeinated drinks, calcium, iron and antacids can disturb how well the medicine is absorbed.

The NHS page also lists calcium and iron supplements and antidepressants such as sertraline among medicines that can interact with levothyroxine.

sections.heading: Is levothyroxine used in pregnancy and breastfeeding?
sections.body:
The NHS says levothyroxine can be taken in pregnancy if needed. Extra blood tests may be needed to check thyroid hormone levels and that the amount suits the person. A UK hospital leaflet notes that the amount often has to be raised early in pregnancy, and that most women return to their earlier amount after the birth.

The NHS says levothyroxine can usually be taken while breastfeeding, but advises checking with a pharmacist or doctor first.

faqs.q: Will I need levothyroxine for life?
faqs.a: The NHS says treatment for an underactive thyroid usually carries on for the rest of a person's life. Blood tests are used at first to find the right amount, and once the result is steady a yearly check is usual. MedlinePlus says people are told to keep taking it when they feel well and not to stop without speaking to their doctor.

faqs.q: Is levothyroxine used for weight loss?
faqs.a: MedlinePlus, a US source, warns against using levothyroxine to lose weight. It says large amounts, especially taken with amphetamines, can cause serious or life-threatening harm. The medicine is prescribed to replace a missing hormone, and the dose is checked with blood tests.

faqs.q: What happens if a dose is missed or too much is taken?
faqs.a: The NHS says a missed dose is taken once remembered, unless the next one is nearly due, in which case the missed one is skipped. It advises against taking two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. A Sheffield Children's leaflet says an extra dose given to a child by mistake is unlikely to cause harm. For taking more than prescribed, the NHS says to speak to a pharmacist as soon as possible, or call NHS 111 if none can be reached or the extra was taken on purpose.

faqs.q: Do other medicines or supplements affect levothyroxine?
faqs.a: Some can. An NHS trust leaflet says calcium, iron and antacids can disturb absorption, and the NHS page lists calcium and iron supplements and antidepressants such as sertraline among those to be aware of. A pharmacist or doctor can check any new medicine, supplement or herbal product against levothyroxine.

faqs.q: What tests are used while taking levothyroxine?
faqs.a: Blood tests are used to check that the amount suits the person, and the results guide any change. Once the result is stable the NHS says a yearly test is usual.

salbutamol.name: Salbutamol
salbutamol.summary: The blue reliever inhaler: a short-acting beta-2 agonist that opens the airways within minutes to relieve asthma and COPD symptoms during an attack or before exercise. The NHS describes it as very effective when used properly, with few side effects beyond a brief tremor and a faster heartbeat, but it relieves the narrowing without treating the inflammation beneath it, so needing it often is itself a warning that the asthma is not controlled.
usedFor: Relief of wheeze and breathlessness in asthma and COPD ('reliever')
Before exercise in exercise-induced asthma
Nebulised or intravenous in severe asthma attacks and COPD flares
Lowering high potassium in emergencies (nebulised)

Known as albuterol in the United States, where it is supplied as pressurised aerosol inhalers, a dry powder inhaler and a nebuliser solution, with combination inhalers pairing it with ipratropium (for COPD) or with the steroid budesonide
salbutamol.howItWorks: Stimulates beta-2 adrenergic receptors on the smooth muscle wrapped around the bronchi. This raises cyclic AMP inside the muscle cells, relaxing them within minutes so the airways widen and air moves more freely. It relieves the narrowing but does nothing for the underlying inflammation, which is why needing it more than twice a week signals poorly controlled asthma and the need for a preventer. The NHS describes it as a bronchodilator that loosens the muscles lining the airways so that breathing becomes easier, starting almost immediately after a puff and continuing to work for some hours; US information puts it as opening the air passages to the lungs. The same beta-2 receptors exist outside the airways, on skeletal muscle, blood vessels and the heart, and on the cells that move potassium into cells, which explains the side effects: a fine tremor of the hands, a faster heartbeat, cramps and, at high doses, a fall in blood potassium. The effect wears off after a few hours, so it is used when symptoms occur rather than on a schedule, and a reliever that is needed several times a day, or that does not bring an attack under control, is a sign that the airways are inflamed and swollen in a way a bronchodilator alone cannot fix; the NHS advises that a person whose breathing does not improve after using the inhaler during an attack needs emergency help. Used for years it causes no lasting damage to the lungs; the risk lies in relying on it instead of treating the inflammation.
salbutamol.onset: Within 5 minutes, peak 15-30 minutes, lasts 4-6 hours. The NHS describes the effect as starting almost immediately after a puff.

common: Fine tremor, fast heartbeat, palpitations, headache: the NHS notes that shakiness of the hands usually wears off after a short time, and that a regularly faster heartbeat is a reason to have the treatment reviewed
Feeling shaky, nervous or restless; muscle cramps; these often improve and disappear after a few days or weeks of use
Dizziness, during which driving, cycling and using machinery are avoided
Using too much causes a racing heart and shakiness
serious: Low potassium with high doses (with steroids, diuretics, theophylline): muscle pain or weakness, cramps, or an irregular or more noticeable heartbeat can be the signs
Arrhythmias in people with heart disease at high doses: a fast, irregular heartbeat that does not settle, or very bad dizziness, needs medical help

Paradoxical bronchospasm (rare); over-reliance masking worsening asthma, linked to asthma deaths: needing the inhaler several times in a day can mean the condition is getting worse and different treatment is needed, and breathing that does not improve after using it is an emergency (999)
Serious allergic reaction (rare): sudden swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue or struggling to breathe needs a 999 call

cautions: Using more than three canisters a year, or needing it daily, means the asthma plan needs review
Anti-inflammatory reliever (budesonide-formoterol) is now preferred as the sole reliever in many guidelines
Inhaler technique matters: slow deep breath, hold for 10 seconds; spacers for children and during attacks
Beta blockers antagonise the effect
Not stopped unless a doctor advises, because breathing problems can worsen; there is no evidence of lasting harm from years of use, and alcohol and food do not interact

Pressurised canisters are labelled with the number of doses they contain and are discarded once that count is reached even if propellant remains, and an aerosol inhaler device is used only with the medicine it was designed for
salbutamol.monitoring: Peak flow and symptom diary; frequency of use as a marker of control. The NHS treats how often the reliever is needed as the key signal: a faster heartbeat that recurs, or needing the inhaler several times a day, prompts a review of the whole asthma plan rather than more reliever, and potassium is checked when high or repeated doses are given in hospital.

sections.heading: What is salbutamol used for?
sections.body:
Salbutamol is a reliever inhaler, the kind many people know as the blue inhaler. The NHS describes it as a medicine that makes breathing easier when asthma or other breathing conditions cause wheezing and breathlessness. It is also used for symptoms of long-term lung conditions such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).

According to the NHS, a reliever works quickly to ease symptoms, and people with asthma are also given a preventer inhaler that is used every day to help stop symptoms. The NHS adds that keeping a diary of how often the reliever is used helps when talking about asthma or COPD control with a doctor or nurse.

sections.heading: How does a salbutamol inhaler work?
sections.body:
Salbutamol is a bronchodilator, which means it relaxes the muscles around the airways so they widen. The NHS says it works almost straight away after a puff and keeps working for a few hours.

Pressurised (metered-dose) inhalers, sometimes called puffers, contain hydrofluorocarbon propellants, while dry powder inhalers do not. The NHS says a person may be asked whether switching to a more environmentally friendly inhaler would suit them.

sections.heading: What are the side effects of salbutamol?
sections.body:
The NHS describes salbutamol as very effective with few side effects when it is used properly. Common side effects, which the NHS says affect more than 1 in 100 people, are feeling shaky, a faster heartbeat and headaches. Salbutamol can also cause dizziness or shakiness, and the NHS advises not to drive, cycle or use tools or machinery until feeling better.

Using too much can make the heart beat faster than normal and cause shakiness. The NHS says to contact NHS 111 about a fast or noticeably pounding heartbeat after using too much, and to call 999 if there is chest pain. Serious side effects are rare. The NHS lists muscle pain or weakness, muscle cramps, a fast irregular heartbeat that does not settle, and very bad dizziness as warning signs, and it says new or worsening breathlessness or chest pain needs a 999 call or a trip to A&E. A serious allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) is also possible. Sudden swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue is one sign, and it needs an emergency 999 call.

sections.heading: Can I drink alcohol or take salbutamol with other medicines?
sections.body:
The NHS says alcohol is fine and normal eating and drinking can continue while using a salbutamol inhaler. It does not affect contraception, including the combined pill and emergency contraception.

Salbutamol can generally be used with most medicines, but some combinations need care. The NHS says water tablets (diuretics), steroid tablets such as prednisolone, and theophylline or aminophylline can raise the risk of low potassium, and it names beta blockers as another combination that can cause problems. The NHS also says there is not enough information on how herbal remedies and supplements interact with salbutamol, and it advises checking with a pharmacist or doctor before starting any new medicine, herbal remedy or supplement.

sections.heading: Who needs extra care with salbutamol, and is it used in pregnancy?
sections.body:
The NHS says most adults and children can use salbutamol inhalers. Extra advice is suggested for people who have had an allergy to salbutamol or other medicines, or who have heart problems, an overactive thyroid, low potassium in the blood or diabetes.

The NHS says salbutamol can be used in pregnancy, and stresses the importance of keeping asthma under control. For breastfeeding, the NHS says the inhaler can be used as normal. It says the amount reaching breast milk is not known but is likely to be very low, and that it has been used this way for many years without side effects in babies. The NHS also says there is no evidence that salbutamol affects fertility in men or women.

sections.heading: What if I need my inhaler more often or have an asthma attack?
sections.body:
The NHS says that needing salbutamol more often than usual can mean a condition is getting worse, and it advises speaking to a doctor, pharmacist or nurse.

For an asthma attack, the NHS says to call 999 if breathing does not improve after using the reliever inhaler. Asthma and Lung UK says to call 999 if the reliever is not helping or the person feels worse at any point, and that calling an ambulance means treatment can start on the way to hospital. After an attack that was managed with the reliever alone, Asthma and Lung UK advises asking for an urgent same-day appointment with a GP or nurse.

faqs.q: Does using a salbutamol inhaler for many years cause harm?
faqs.a: The NHS says there is no evidence that salbutamol does any lasting damage to the body, even if it is used for many years. Needing it more often than usual can be a sign that a condition is getting worse, and the NHS advises speaking to a doctor, pharmacist or nurse about that.

faqs.q: Can I drive after using my blue inhaler?
faqs.a: The NHS says salbutamol can cause dizziness or shakiness in some people. If that happens, it advises not to drive, cycle or use tools or machinery until feeling better, and says that anyone in doubt should not drive.

faqs.q: What happens if I use too much salbutamol?
faqs.a: Using too much can make the heart beat faster than normal and cause shakiness. The NHS says to contact NHS 111 about a fast or noticeably pounding heartbeat after using too much, and to call 999 if there is chest pain.

faqs.q: Does salbutamol affect contraception?
faqs.a: According to the NHS, salbutamol does not affect any type of contraception. This includes the combined pill and emergency contraception. The NHS also says alcohol is fine and normal eating and drinking can continue while using the inhaler.

faqs.q: Is salbutamol an emergency treatment?
faqs.a: The reliever inhaler is what the NHS and Asthma and Lung UK describe using during an asthma attack. The NHS says that if breathing does not improve after using it, a 999 call is needed. Needing it more often than usual is a reason to speak to a doctor, pharmacist or nurse.

inhaled-corticosteroids.name: Inhaled corticosteroids
inhaled-corticosteroids.summary: The preventer inhalers of asthma: low doses of steroid delivered straight into the airways damp down inflammation so attacks become rarer and milder. They do nothing for an attack that is already happening, work only when used every day, and because so little reaches the rest of the body their main side effects are a sore mouth and hoarse voice rather than the whole-body effects of steroid tablets.
inhaled-corticosteroids.class: Inhaled glucocorticoid (with or without a long-acting beta-2 agonist)
usedFor: The cornerstone of asthma treatment: daily to prevent attacks and control symptoms, described in US sources as the first-choice treatment for preventing exacerbations in persistent asthma
COPD with frequent exacerbations and high blood eosinophils, combined with long-acting bronchodilators
Combined inhalers with formoterol used as both preventer and reliever (MART regimens)
Stepped up (or combined with a long-acting beta-2 agonist or a leukotriene receptor antagonist) when symptoms are not controlled, and stepped down at review when they are
inhaled-corticosteroids.howItWorks: Steroid molecules deposited on the airway lining diffuse into cells and bind glucocorticoid receptors, which move to the nucleus and switch off the genes for inflammatory cytokines, reduce eosinophils and mast cells, and shrink mucosal swelling and mucus. Inhaling delivers a tiny dose straight to the airways, so the whole-body effects of steroid tablets are largely avoided. Benefit builds over days to weeks and depends on daily use. The NHS describes the preventer as calming the immune system and reducing the swelling in the lungs that makes breathing difficult; this is different from a reliever, which opens the airways within minutes, and a steroid inhaler on its own cannot treat a sudden attack of coughing, wheezing and breathlessness. Some combination inhalers pair the steroid with formoterol, a long-acting bronchodilator that also acts quickly, which is why those particular products can be used both as a daily preventer and as the reliever. Protection accumulates: many people notice a difference within days but the full benefit takes weeks, and it fades if the inhaler is stopped, so it is not stopped suddenly without advice. Dose tiers (low, medium and high) match asthma severity, and the lowest dose that keeps control is used.
inhaled-corticosteroids.onset: Does not work straight away: symptoms improve over 1-2 weeks; full effect at 4-8 weeks, and only with daily use.

common: Oral thrush (white patches, redness and soreness in the mouth) and a hoarse voice: rinsing the mouth or brushing the teeth after each dose and using a spacer with a pressurised inhaler reduce the risk
Dry or sore throat, cough on inhaling
serious: Pneumonia risk in COPD at higher doses

At high doses long term (more than a few months): adrenal suppression, Cushingoid changes (a rounded 'moon face', weight gain over the upper back or abdomen developing gradually), reduced bone density, cataract and glaucoma, easy bruising, a small effect on growth velocity in children that is minimal at low doses

Adrenal insufficiency is more likely at high doses, with other steroid medicines, or with tablets for fungal infections or HIV that slow the steroid's breakdown; sudden stopping of high doses can unmask it
Breathing that does not improve or worsens despite the inhaler, which needs prompt review rather than more doses

cautions: Use the lowest dose that keeps control, stepped up or down at review
Long-acting beta agonists must never be used alone in asthma without a steroid
Carry a steroid card at high doses; check bone density if on high dose for years
Technique check at every review; a spacer is recommended for high doses given through a pressurised metered-dose inhaler because it improves delivery and lessens mouth and throat side effects
Not stopped abruptly: the NHS advises speaking to a doctor or nurse first, because protection is lost and, after high doses, adrenal function may need time to recover
Tell the prescriber about antifungal tablets, HIV medicines or other steroids, which raise the risk of whole-body steroid effects
inhaled-corticosteroids.monitoring: Symptom control, reliever use, peak flow; growth in children; annual review. The review also checks inhaler technique and adherence, looks in the mouth for thrush, and asks about hoarseness; at high doses for prolonged periods clinicians watch for Cushingoid features and consider adrenal function, bone density and eye checks.

omeprazole.name: Omeprazole
omeprazole.summary: A proton pump inhibitor that switches off acid production in the stomach, healing ulcers and reflux oesophagitis and protecting the stomach from anti-inflammatory drugs.
usedFor: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease and its complications (oesophagitis, Barrett oesophagus)
Healing stomach and duodenal ulcers; part of H. pylori eradication triple therapy

omeprazole.howItWorks: Irreversibly blocks the hydrogen-potassium ATPase, the 'proton pump' in the parietal cells of the stomach lining that secretes acid as the final step of every stimulus. Because the pump is disabled rather than the signals, acid falls by over 90%, and new pumps must be made before secretion recovers, so the effect outlasts the drug's short half-life. Given 30-60 minutes before breakfast, when pumps are most active.
omeprazole.onset: Acid suppression within hours; maximal after 3-5 days. Symptom relief in reflux within days.

common: Headache, nausea, diarrhoea, constipation, abdominal pain
Wind, dizziness
serious: Low magnesium with long-term use (cramps, arrhythmia)
Clostridioides difficile and other gut infections, and pneumonia (acid normally kills swallowed microbes)
Reduced absorption of B12, iron and calcium; a modest increase in fractures with prolonged high-dose use
Acute interstitial nephritis and, rarely, subacute cutaneous lupus

cautions: Use the lowest effective dose and review long-term use; rebound acid hypersecretion for a few weeks after stopping
May mask stomach cancer symptoms: alarm features (weight loss, swallowing difficulty, bleeding, age over 55 with new symptoms) need endoscopy first
Omeprazole reduces the activation of clopidogrel (pantoprazole preferred); for a breath or stool H. pylori test it is usually paused for two weeks, as directed by the clinician arranging the test
Interactions with methotrexate, some HIV drugs
omeprazole.monitoring: Magnesium and B12 if used for more than a year; kidney function if symptoms of nephritis.

omeprazole.understand: Omeprazole switches off the acid pumps in the cells of your stomach lining, so far less acid is made. With less acid, ulcers can heal, the oesophagus is no longer burned by reflux, and the stomach is protected from anti-inflammatory painkillers.
omeprazole.mechanismDetail: Omeprazole is a substituted benzimidazole prodrug. Absorbed from gastro-resistant granules, it concentrates in the acidic secretory canaliculi of gastric parietal cells, where it is protonated and converted to a sulfenamide that forms covalent disulphide bonds with cysteines on the H+/K+ ATPase, inhibiting the pump irreversibly. Because the pump is the final step of acid secretion, basal and stimulated acid output fall by more than 90%; secretion recovers only as new pumps are synthesised (half-life of pump turnover about 50 hours), so once-daily dosing before breakfast gives a sustained effect despite a plasma half-life of about an hour. Omeprazole is metabolised by CYP2C19 and CYP3A4 and inhibits CYP2C19, reducing activation of clopidogrel and raising levels of some other drugs. Long-term acid suppression raises gastrin, alters absorption of magnesium, calcium, iron and vitamin B12, and changes the gut microbiome.

sections.heading: What is omeprazole used for?
sections.body:
Omeprazole is a proton pump inhibitor, a medicine that lowers the amount of acid the stomach makes. The NHS says it is used to treat or prevent stomach ulcers, heartburn and gastro-oesophageal reflux disease, often called GORD. It is also used, together with antibiotics, to treat a stomach infection called Helicobacter pylori.

Omeprazole comes as capsules, tablets and a liquid, and the NHS says tablets and capsules are swallowed whole with water or squash. The NHS says capsules are prescription only, while some tablets can be bought from pharmacies and supermarkets for adults. Tablets bought this way are meant for short-term use, and the NHS says to tell a doctor if symptoms persist. The NHS describes omeprazole as a medicine to treat heartburn and indigestion.

sections.heading: How does omeprazole work, and how quickly?
sections.body:
Omeprazole blocks the last step in the making of stomach acid. It acts on an enzyme called the proton pump, which sits on acid-making cells in the stomach wall. A review of its pharmacology says omeprazole is a prodrug, changed to its active form only in the acid-making cells, where it binds irreversibly to the proton pump. This gives an effective and long-lasting reduction in stomach acid.

The NHS says omeprazole starts to work within 2 to 3 days, but it may take up to 4 weeks to work fully. It is a medicine that lowers stomach acid, and the NHS lists ulcers, heartburn and GORD among the conditions it treats or prevents.

sections.heading: What are the side effects of omeprazole?
sections.body:
The NHS lists headache, stomach pain, feeling or being sick, constipation and diarrhoea as common side effects. The NHS says omeprazole can also cause dizziness, sleepiness or blurred vision, and advises against driving, cycling or using machinery or tools until feeling better.

Serious side effects are rarer. The NHS says omeprazole may affect how the body absorbs vitamin B12, particularly with long use, that taking it for more than a year may raise the chance of bone fractures, and that a serious allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) is possible in rare cases. The NHS says the level of magnesium in the blood may also fall with longer use. Anaphylaxis is a medical emergency, and the route for that in the UK is 999.

The NHS says to speak to a doctor about trouble swallowing, feeling or being sick, feeling full very quickly when eating, or losing weight without trying, because these can be signs of stomach cancer.

sections.heading: Taking omeprazole with other medicines or alcohol
sections.body:
The NHS says omeprazole can interact with other medicines, so a pharmacist or doctor can be asked about anything new. UK drug safety guidance discourages using omeprazole or esomeprazole with clopidogrel, an antiplatelet medicine. The Specialist Pharmacy Service, part of the NHS, explains that clopidogrel is activated by an enzyme called CYP2C19, and that omeprazole and esomeprazole inhibit this enzyme, which can lower the level of activated clopidogrel. The Specialist Pharmacy Service says lansoprazole, pantoprazole or rabeprazole are preferred to omeprazole for people taking clopidogrel.

The NHS says alcohol does not stop omeprazole working. But alcohol makes the stomach produce more acid than usual, which can irritate the stomach lining and make symptoms worse. For that reason the NHS says it is best to avoid alcohol if possible while taking omeprazole.

sections.heading: Who needs extra care with omeprazole?
sections.body:
The NHS lists kidney conditions, liver conditions, osteoporosis, and a past allergic reaction or serious side effect from omeprazole or another proton pump inhibitor as reasons to check with a doctor or pharmacist before taking it. The NHS says that after more than a year of omeprazole, a doctor will regularly check health to see whether to carry on.

The NHS says omeprazole can usually be taken in pregnancy, but a pharmacist or doctor should be asked first. It suggests trying to ease indigestion without medicine first. On breastfeeding, the NHS says omeprazole passes into breast milk in small amounts, and that it is OK to take while breastfeeding if a doctor or health visitor says the baby is healthy. The NHS says there is no clear evidence that omeprazole lowers fertility in men or women.

faqs.q: Can I buy omeprazole without a prescription?
faqs.a: The NHS says some omeprazole tablets can be bought from pharmacies and supermarkets for adults, while capsules are prescription only. Tablets bought this way are meant for short-term use. The NHS says to tell a doctor if symptoms persist, and that a doctor may order tests or suggest a different medicine.

faqs.q: How long does omeprazole take to work?
faqs.a: The NHS says omeprazole starts to work within 2 to 3 days, but it may take up to 4 weeks to work fully. Tablets bought from a pharmacy are meant for short-term use, and the NHS says to tell a doctor if symptoms persist. The NHS also says it is not known whether omeprazole works less well the longer it is taken.

faqs.q: Can I drink alcohol while taking omeprazole?
faqs.a: The NHS says alcohol does not interfere with how omeprazole works. However, alcohol makes the stomach produce more acid than usual. That extra acid can irritate the stomach lining and make symptoms worse. The NHS therefore says it is best to avoid alcohol if possible while taking omeprazole.

faqs.q: What does the NHS say about long-term use of omeprazole?
faqs.a: The NHS says taking omeprazole for more than a year may raise the chance of bone fractures and gut infections. It may also affect how the body absorbs vitamin B12. The NHS says a doctor will regularly check health after a year to see whether to carry on. The NHS also says magnesium levels in the blood may fall with longer use.

faqs.q: Which symptoms does the NHS say to mention to a doctor while taking omeprazole?
faqs.a: The NHS says to speak to a doctor about trouble swallowing, feeling or being sick, feeling full very quickly when eating, or losing weight without trying, because these can be signs of stomach cancer. The NHS also says a doctor will regularly check health after a year of omeprazole, to see whether to carry on.

amoxicillin.name: Amoxicillin
amoxicillin.summary: A widely used penicillin antibiotic that kills bacteria by breaking their cell walls, prescribed for chest, ear, sinus, dental and some urinary infections and as part of Helicobacter pylori treatment; without effect on viruses and not used in people with a history of true penicillin allergy.
usedFor: Chest infections and community-acquired pneumonia

amoxicillin.howItWorks: Binds the penicillin-binding proteins that bacteria use to cross-link the peptidoglycan of their cell wall. Growing bacteria with a weakened wall burst under their own osmotic pressure. Human cells have no cell wall, which is why penicillins are so selective. Bacteria fight back with beta-lactamase enzymes that destroy the drug; clavulanic acid (in co-amoxiclav) blocks that enzyme. Antibiotics do nothing against viruses, the cause of most sore throats, colds and coughs.
amoxicillin.onset: Improvement within 48-72 hours; the full course is decided by the infection, not by symptoms.

common: Nausea, diarrhoea, thrush
Non-allergic rash (very common in glandular fever, where amoxicillin should be avoided)
serious: Anaphylaxis in true penicillin allergy (about 1 in 10,000 courses); most reported 'penicillin allergies' are not true allergy and can be safely delabelled

Liver injury with co-amoxiclav (cholestatic hepatitis), seizures at very high doses in kidney failure
Antimicrobial resistance across the population with every unnecessary course

amoxicillin.understand: Amoxicillin attacks the wall that holds a bacterium together. Growing bacteria with a damaged wall burst and die. Human cells have no such wall, so the drug leaves them alone, but it also cannot touch viruses, which have no wall either.
amoxicillin.mechanismDetail: Amoxicillin is an aminopenicillin, a beta-lactam that binds and inactivates penicillin-binding proteins (transpeptidases) in the bacterial cytoplasmic membrane, preventing cross-linking of peptidoglycan during cell-wall synthesis; autolytic enzymes then lyse the growing cell, so the effect is bactericidal and time-dependent (efficacy depends on the time the concentration stays above the MIC, hence three-times-daily dosing). Its spectrum covers streptococci including most pneumococci, many enterococci, Listeria, Haemophilus (non-beta-lactamase producers), Helicobacter pylori and some Enterobacterales, but it is destroyed by beta-lactamases; clavulanic acid in co-amoxiclav inhibits many of them. Amoxicillin is better absorbed orally than ampicillin and is excreted largely unchanged by the kidney, so doses are reduced in severe renal impairment and levels are raised by probenecid.

Antimicrobial resistance: every unnecessary course selects resistant bacteria; the drug does not treat viral sore throats, colds or most coughs, and the course is completed as prescribed.
