sections.heading: What is amoxicillin used for?
sections.body:
Amoxicillin is a penicillin antibiotic, a medicine that treats infections caused by bacteria. The NHS says it is used for chest infections, including pneumonia, and for dental abscesses. It is often prescribed for children with ear infections. The NHS also says it can be used with other medicines for stomach ulcers.

In the UK it needs a prescription. It comes as capsules or a liquid, and the NHS says injections are usually given only in hospital. The NHS says most adults and children can take amoxicillin. For most infections, the NHS says people should feel better within a few days.

Antibiotics only work on infections caused by bacteria. They have no effect on viral illnesses such as colds and flu.

sections.heading: How does amoxicillin work?
sections.body:
Amoxicillin belongs to the penicillin group of antibiotics. Penicillin antibiotics kill susceptible bacteria by blocking an enzyme that completes the building of the bacterial cell wall.

The NHS says to tell a doctor if there is no improvement after a few days, or if symptoms get worse at any point. NHS Shropshire, Telford and Wrekin advises taking antibiotics exactly as prescribed, including the full course, and never saving them for later or sharing them with others.

Unnecessary use of antibiotics can cause some bacteria to become resistant to them, which is called antimicrobial resistance. A practice page adds that routine procedures such as surgery, cancer treatment and organ transplants become riskier as antibiotics lose their effect.

sections.heading: What are the side effects of amoxicillin?
sections.body:
The NHS lists feeling sick and diarrhoea as the most common side effects. It also says thrush can occur after antibiotics.

The NHS says to call a doctor or NHS 111 now for diarrhoea that is severe or that contains blood or mucus. It lists signs of liver problems among the serious effects, such as yellowing of the skin or eyes, and pale poo with dark urine. Some of these serious effects can appear up to two months after the course has finished.

Delayed allergic reactions can happen several days after taking amoxicillin capsules. The NHS says these are usually a mild skin rash, though a high temperature, joint pain and swollen glands can also occur.

sections.heading: Allergy and who needs extra care with amoxicillin
sections.body:
In rare cases, amoxicillin can cause a serious allergic reaction called anaphylaxis. The NHS says signs include swelling of the face, lips, tongue or throat and difficulty breathing, and that anaphylaxis needs emergency treatment. In the UK, 999 is the number to call in an emergency.

The NHS lists a past allergic reaction to amoxicillin, penicillin or another medicine among the things to tell a doctor about before taking amoxicillin. The UK product information says a doctor should ask carefully about earlier allergic reactions to penicillins, cephalosporins or other related antibiotics before treatment starts.

The NHS says to check with a doctor or pharmacist before taking amoxicillin. It advises telling a doctor first about liver or kidney problems, upcoming blood or urine tests, and recent or upcoming vaccinations. Glandular fever is also on that list, because amoxicillin can cause a rash in people who have it.

The NHS says amoxicillin can be taken during pregnancy, while advising a check with a pharmacist or doctor first. It also says amoxicillin can be taken while breastfeeding, because only tiny amounts get into breast milk.

sections.heading: Taking amoxicillin with other medicines or alcohol
sections.body:
The NHS says alcohol can be drunk while taking amoxicillin. UK product information lists some medicines that can interact with amoxicillin. Allopurinol may make allergic skin reactions more likely. Probenecid reduces the kidneys' removal of amoxicillin, which can raise and prolong its levels in the blood, and the product information says using the two together is not recommended. Blood thinners such as warfarin may call for extra blood tests. Methotrexate may increase side effects, and other antibiotics such as tetracycline may make amoxicillin work less well.

The NHS says amoxicillin does not stop any type of contraception working, including the combined pill, the progestogen-only pill and emergency contraception. However, being sick or having severe or long-lasting diarrhoea may stop contraceptive pills protecting against pregnancy. The NHS says amoxicillin should not affect the ability to drive or cycle.

faqs.q: Can alcohol be drunk while taking amoxicillin?
faqs.a: The NHS says alcohol can be drunk while taking amoxicillin. It also says amoxicillin should not affect the ability to drive or cycle. The most common side effects the NHS lists are feeling sick and diarrhoea, and the NHS says thrush can occur after antibiotics. These answers come from the NHS page about amoxicillin itself.

faqs.q: Does amoxicillin work for colds and flu?
faqs.a: No, antibiotics only work on infections caused by bacteria. Colds and flu are viral illnesses, and antibiotics have no effect on them. The NHS says GPs do not recommend antibiotics for colds and flu because they will not relieve symptoms or speed up recovery. Unnecessary use of antibiotics can cause some bacteria to become resistant to them, which is called antimicrobial resistance.

faqs.q: What if amoxicillin does not seem to help?
faqs.a: The NHS says to tell a doctor if there is no improvement after a few days, or if symptoms get worse at any point. For most infections, the NHS says people should feel better within a few days. NHS Shropshire, Telford and Wrekin advises taking antibiotics exactly as prescribed, including the full course.

faqs.q: Does amoxicillin affect the contraceptive pill?
faqs.a: The NHS says amoxicillin does not stop any type of contraception working, including the combined pill, the progestogen-only pill and emergency contraception. The exception is when it makes someone sick or causes severe or long-lasting diarrhoea, because contraceptive pills may then not protect against pregnancy.

faqs.q: What can cause a rash during amoxicillin treatment?
faqs.a: The NHS says amoxicillin can cause a rash in people with glandular fever. Delayed allergic reactions can happen several days after taking amoxicillin capsules and are usually a mild skin rash, though a high temperature, joint pain and swollen glands can also occur. Swelling of the face, lips, tongue or throat, or difficulty breathing, may be anaphylaxis, which needs emergency treatment: call 999.

cetirizine.name: Cetirizine and antihistamines
cetirizine.summary: A second-generation (less sedating) antihistamine that blocks histamine H1 receptors to relieve hay fever, hives and other allergic symptoms. It works within about an hour, is taken once a day and is sold without prescription, but it can cause drowsiness in some people and is an add-on, never a substitute for adrenaline, in anaphylaxis.
usedFor: Hay fever and year-round allergic rhinitis: sneezing, runny nose, itchy or watery eyes; also allergic conjunctivitis
Urticaria (hives), itching and the itch of eczema
Mild allergic reactions to foods, insect bites and drugs (not a substitute for adrenaline in anaphylaxis)
Sedating first-generation antihistamines (chlorphenamine, promethazine) for short-term itch or nausea
cetirizine.howItWorks: Blocks H1 histamine receptors on blood vessels, nerves and smooth muscle. When mast cells release histamine in response to an allergen, it normally makes capillaries leak (swelling, runny nose), stimulates itch nerves and constricts airways; with the receptors occupied, those effects are muted. Second-generation drugs cross the blood-brain barrier poorly, so they cause much less drowsiness than older ones. The NHS puts it this way: on contact with something a person is allergic to, such as pollen or animal fur, the body produces histamine, and cetirizine works by blocking its effects, so symptoms begin to ease within an hour. It treats the symptoms rather than the allergy itself, so it is taken for as long as exposure continues (a pollen season, a flare of hives) and can be used daily over long periods. Among the non-sedating antihistamines, cetirizine is the one most likely to cause sleepiness; loratadine, desloratadine and fexofenadine are less so, which guides the choice for drivers and shift workers. Cetirizine also exists as eye drops for itchy allergic conjunctivitis and, in some countries, as an intravenous injection for acute hives given by a healthcare professional.
cetirizine.onset: Within an hour; lasts 24 hours, so it is taken once a day.

common: Feeling sleepy or tired (about 1 in 10 people, and more than with loratadine or fexofenadine)
Headache, dry mouth, feeling sick, dizziness, diarrhoea; getting up slowly helps dizziness, and driving, cycling or using machinery is avoided while dizzy or drowsy
Severe or prolonged diarrhoea or vomiting can reduce the protection of contraceptive pills
serious: Rare serious allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) to the medicine itself: sudden swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue needs an emergency (999) call
Unusual bruising or bleeding that is slow to stop, which the NHS advises reporting to a doctor or NHS 111
Marked sedation and impaired driving with first-generation agents; confusion and falls in the elderly, urinary retention in men with prostate enlargement
QT prolongation with some older non-sedating agents (withdrawn)
Severe itching on stopping suddenly after long regular use (a very small risk, so a doctor is consulted before stopping long-term daily treatment)

cautions: Check driving response with any antihistamine; avoid or limit alcohol, which adds to the drowsiness
Dose reduced in kidney impairment for cetirizine
Not for children under 2 without advice; sedating antihistamines avoided in young children
Anaphylaxis needs adrenaline first: antihistamines are adjuncts only
Long-term daily use is regarded as safe, but the NHS advises using it only for as long as it is needed and checking with a doctor before stopping after prolonged regular use
cetirizine.monitoring: None. No blood tests are needed; the only follow-up is checking that symptoms are controlled and that drowsiness is not interfering with driving, work or school, and reviewing whether the medicine is still needed once the allergen exposure has passed.

sertraline.name: Sertraline and SSRIs
sertraline.summary: A selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) antidepressant used for depression, anxiety disorders, panic and obsessive-compulsive disorder; it takes several weeks to work fully. The first weeks are often the hardest, with nausea, headache, poor sleep and sometimes worse anxiety before mood improves, so early review matters; once established it is usually continued for months after recovery and then reduced gradually rather than stopped suddenly.
usedFor: Moderate to severe depression, alongside psychological therapy
Anxiety disorders: generalised anxiety, panic disorder, social anxiety, PTSD, OCD; US labelling also covers premenstrual dysphoric disorder
Sertraline is a first choice after a heart attack because of its cardiac safety
One of the better-studied antidepressants in pregnancy, so it is often the SSRI chosen when treatment is needed during pregnancy
sertraline.howItWorks: Blocks the serotonin transporter that pumps serotonin back into the nerve ending after release, so more remains in the synapse. The immediate rise in serotonin is not itself the cure: over weeks, receptors adapt, and growth factors such as BDNF and neuroplasticity in the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex increase, which is thought to underlie the delayed improvement in mood and anxiety. The NHS describes it for the reader as increasing the levels of a mood-enhancing chemical called serotonin in the brain, and US information as increasing the amount of serotonin, a natural substance that helps maintain mental balance. The gap between the chemical effect (hours) and the clinical effect (weeks) explains the characteristic early course: side effects such as nausea, headache and disturbed sleep appear first, some people, especially those treated for panic, find their anxiety worse for the first few weeks, and the full benefit takes several weeks. Serotonin also acts outside the brain, on the gut (nausea and diarrhoea), on platelets (easier bleeding, especially with anti-inflammatory painkillers or anticoagulants) and on sexual function, which accounts for the main side effects. Because the brain adapts to the raised serotonin, stopping abruptly produces discontinuation symptoms, so the dose is reduced gradually under supervision, and combining it with other serotonin-raising medicines can tip the balance into serotonin syndrome.
sertraline.onset: Side effects first; mood benefit begins at 2-4 weeks, full at 6-8 weeks. Continued for at least 6 months after recovery. The NHS notes that anxiety can be worse before it is better.

common: Nausea, diarrhoea, headache, sweating, insomnia or drowsiness in the first weeks; the NHS adds dry mouth and weight gain, notes that most of these ease after a couple of weeks, and suggests taking the dose with food for nausea, in the morning if it disturbs sleep and in the evening if it causes drowsiness
Sexual dysfunction (reduced libido, delayed orgasm), which often persists
Increased anxiety and agitation at the start, particularly in people treated for panic attacks; this usually wears off after a few weeks
Dizziness or drowsiness, during which driving, cycling and using machinery are avoided
serious: Increased suicidal thoughts in the first weeks, particularly under 25: close follow-up. New or worsening thoughts of suicide or self-harm, or marked agitation, need urgent contact with a GP or NHS 111, and 999 or A&E if in immediate danger (Samaritans: 116 123, free, any time)
Bleeding risk, especially with NSAIDs, aspirin or anticoagulants (serotonin is needed for platelet function)

Low sodium in the elderly; serotonin syndrome with tramadol, triptans, MAOIs, St John's wort: a rare but serious reaction with a fast heartbeat, sweating, shaking, twitching muscles and confusion or agitation, which the NHS describes as needing urgent help
Discontinuation symptoms (dizziness, electric-shock sensations, irritability) if stopped abruptly: taper over weeks
Mania: feeling unusually high, full of energy or unable to sleep
Serious allergic reaction (anaphylaxis), which is rare

cautions: Review within 1-2 weeks of starting, sooner in young people
Do not stop suddenly: the NHS describes the doctor recommending a gradual reduction to prevent withdrawal side effects
Citalopram and escitalopram prolong the QT interval: dose limits and ECG in heart disease

Pregnancy: discuss risks and benefits; sertraline is among the better studied. The NHS states it can be used in pregnancy when needed; some studies suggest a possible small effect on the baby's heart development, although most babies are unaffected; use near delivery can cause short-lived withdrawal symptoms and very rarely breathing problems in the newborn, who is checked after birth, and use in the final month slightly raises the risk of bleeding after delivery, which is treatable and not a reason to stop
Grapefruit juice is avoided because it can increase the amount of sertraline in the body and the risk of side effects

SSRIs interact unpredictably with some other medicines, raising the risk of bleeding or serotonin syndrome, so new medicines, including over-the-counter and herbal products, are checked with a pharmacist first
Taken once a day, morning or evening; the liquid concentrate is diluted before use as directed
sertraline.monitoring: Mood and suicidality at review; sodium in the elderly; ECG for citalopram at high doses. Early reviews check for worsening anxiety or agitation, new or increased thoughts of self-harm, sleep and appetite, and whether side effects are settling; later reviews judge response and decide how long to continue after recovery and when to begin a gradual reduction. No routine blood tests are needed for sertraline itself.

sections.heading: What is sertraline used for and how does it work?
sections.body:
Sertraline is an antidepressant from a group called selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, or SSRIs. The NHS says it is often used for depression and sometimes for panic attacks, obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD) and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). MedlinePlus also lists social anxiety disorder among its uses. The NHS says children aged 6 to 17 can also take sertraline, but only for OCD. It comes as tablets.

The NHS says it is not known exactly how antidepressants work. One view is that they increase the levels of brain chemicals called neurotransmitters, mainly serotonin and noradrenaline. The NHS says people may start to feel better after 1 to 2 weeks, but sertraline usually takes 4 to 6 weeks to work fully.

sections.heading: What are the side effects of sertraline?
sections.body:
The NHS lists headaches, feeling sick, dizziness or drowsiness, dry mouth, diarrhoea, problems sleeping and sexual problems among the common side effects of sertraline. The NHS says some of the common side effects gradually improve as the body gets used to the medicine. It also lists agitation, shakiness and anxiety among the early side effects of antidepressants, which generally improve with time.

Serious reactions are rarer. The NHS lists serotonin syndrome and mania among them, and describes serotonin syndrome as an uncommon but potentially serious set of side effects linked to SSRIs.

MedlinePlus warns that sertraline may raise the risk of suicidal thoughts and actions in children, teenagers and young adults, and that the risk may be higher in the first few months of treatment and when the dose is increased. It lists new or worsening depression, thoughts of harming yourself, extreme worry, panic attacks and severe restlessness as warning signs, and advises calling a doctor right away if they appear. The NHS says that anyone who may be about to harm themselves should call 999 or go to A&E. For urgent mental health help, NHS 111 has a mental health option (option 2), and Samaritans is free to call on 116 123 at any time. A GP can also be asked for an emergency appointment.

sections.heading: Who needs extra care with sertraline, and what should it not be mixed with?
sections.body:
The NHS says most adults can take sertraline. People who have had an allergic reaction to sertraline or another medicine may not be able to take it. The NHS also lists heart problems, glaucoma and epilepsy as reasons for extra care, because sertraline can affect heart rhythm, raise the pressure in the eye or increase the risk of a seizure. Sertraline can make blood sugar harder to control, so a doctor may suggest checking it more often at first for people with diabetes.

The NHS says it is best not to drink alcohol while taking sertraline, because alcohol can stop the medicine working properly. Grapefruit juice can increase the amount of sertraline in the body and the risk of side effects. The NHS says not to take the herbal remedy St John's wort during treatment, because this increases the risk of side effects, and that there is very little information about other herbal remedies and supplements. The NHS flags medicines that affect the heartbeat, and other antidepressants, as ones to raise with a doctor first. The UK patient leaflet says sertraline must not be used with a group of antidepressants called MAOIs, such as selegiline or moclobemide, or with linezolid.

sections.heading: Can sertraline be taken in pregnancy or while breastfeeding?
sections.body:
The NHS says sertraline can be taken in pregnancy. Some studies have suggested that it might occasionally affect the development of a baby's heart. The NHS says that if there is any risk it is small, and that most babies born to women taking sertraline have a normal heart.

When it is taken in the weeks before delivery, sertraline can sometimes cause short-term withdrawal symptoms in the baby and, very rarely, breathing problems. The NHS says the baby will be checked after birth and given extra care if needed. MedlinePlus advises telling a doctor about a pregnancy, a plan to become pregnant or breastfeeding.

The NHS says that if a doctor or health visitor says the baby is healthy, it is OK to take sertraline while breastfeeding, and describes it as one of the preferred antidepressants during breastfeeding.

sections.heading: How is stopping sertraline managed?
sections.body:
The NHS says stopping sertraline should involve reducing the dose gradually, which helps to prevent withdrawal symptoms. The NHS says this is normally done over several weeks or months, and the pace depends on the medicine, the dose and how long it has been taken. The UK patient leaflet says not to stop taking sertraline unless a doctor says so.

The NHS says withdrawal symptoms usually begin within 5 days of stopping and generally last 1 to 2 weeks, but some people have severe symptoms that last for several months or more. The Royal College of Psychiatrists says withdrawal symptoms usually improve quickly, in days or even hours, if the antidepressant is restarted. The NHS says that if symptoms are severe, a doctor may suggest reducing the dose more slowly or going back to a higher dose before trying again. The NHS also says that once a person feels better, it is likely they will continue to take sertraline for several more months.

faqs.q: How long does sertraline take to work?
faqs.a: The NHS says people may start to feel better after 1 to 2 weeks, and that sertraline usually takes 4 to 6 weeks to work fully. The NHS says some of the common side effects gradually improve as the body gets used to the medicine. It also lists agitation, shakiness and anxiety among the early side effects of antidepressants, which generally improve with time.

faqs.q: Can sertraline be stopped once someone feels better?
faqs.a: The NHS says that once a person feels better, it is likely they will continue to take sertraline for several more months. Stopping should involve reducing the dose gradually, which helps to prevent withdrawal symptoms, and the NHS says this is normally done over several weeks or months. The UK patient leaflet says not to stop taking sertraline unless a doctor says so.

faqs.q: Can sertraline be taken in pregnancy?
faqs.a: The NHS says sertraline can be taken in pregnancy. Some studies have suggested that it might occasionally affect the development of a baby's heart, but the NHS says that if there is any risk it is small. Taken in the weeks before delivery, it can sometimes cause short-term withdrawal symptoms in the baby. The NHS says the baby will be checked after birth and given extra care if needed.

faqs.q: Can sertraline make suicidal thoughts worse?
faqs.a: MedlinePlus warns that sertraline may raise the risk of suicidal thoughts and actions in children, teenagers and young adults, and that the risk may be higher in the first few months and when the dose is increased. The NHS says that anyone who may be about to harm themselves should call 999 or go to A&E. For urgent help, NHS 111 has a mental health option (option 2), and Samaritans is free to call on 116 123 at any time.

prednisolone.name: Prednisolone and steroids
prednisolone.summary: A corticosteroid tablet that suppresses inflammation and the immune system, used in asthma flare-ups, arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease and many autoimmune conditions. Short courses are usually well tolerated, but the longer and higher the course the more the body shows the effects of excess steroid: weight gain, raised blood sugar and pressure, thinning bones, infections and mood change, and a shut-down of the body's own cortisol production that makes sudden stopping dangerous.
usedFor: Asthma attacks and COPD flares (5-day courses)
Flares of rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease, gout, polymyalgia rheumatica, temporal arteritis
Autoimmune disease, severe allergic reactions, some cancers and transplant rejection; US information also lists multiple sclerosis relapses and the symptoms of some cancers
Replacing cortisol in adrenal insufficiency (hydrocortisone); dexamethasone in brain swelling and severe COVID-19
Prednisolone eye drops for inflammation of the eye from allergy, infection, chemical or physical injury and after eye surgery; enemas and suppositories for inflammation of the rectum and lower bowel
prednisolone.howItWorks: A synthetic version of cortisol, the adrenal stress hormone, at doses far above what the body makes. It enters cells and binds glucocorticoid receptors that switch off genes for inflammatory cytokines and switch on anti-inflammatory ones, shrinking the whole inflammatory response, whatever its trigger: it does not treat the cause. The same receptors in liver, muscle, bone, skin and brain produce the side effects, and prolonged dosing suppresses the pituitary-adrenal axis so the body's own cortisol production shuts down. The NHS explains it to the reader as reducing swelling (inflammation) and calming down the immune system, which is why it helps autoimmune conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis, where the immune system attacks the body's own tissues; US information puts it as reducing swelling and redness and changing the way the immune system works. Because the dose is higher than the body's own cortisol output, every tissue that responds to cortisol responds to the medicine: appetite and fluid retention rise, blood sugar and blood pressure drift up, bone is lost, skin thins and mood and sleep change. The suppression of the body's own production is the reason a course of more than a few weeks is tapered rather than stopped: as US information puts it, if the medicine is stopped suddenly the body may not have enough naturally produced steroid to function normally, and the NHS describes withdrawal with tiredness, weakness, body aches and joint pain as well as a flare of the original condition. Taking the dose once in the morning copies the body's own rhythm and reduces sleeplessness.
prednisolone.onset: Anti-inflammatory effect within hours; symptom relief in asthma and arthritis within a day or two. Weight gain becomes likely once a course lasts more than a few weeks, and the long-term harms (bone thinning, diabetes, eye problems, high blood pressure) build with months and years of use.

common: Increased appetite and weight gain, fluid retention, mood change, insomnia: the NHS notes weight gain is likely with courses of more than a few weeks because the medicine increases hunger and water retention, and that a morning dose reduces sleep problems and restlessness
Raised blood glucose (new or worsened diabetes), raised blood pressure
Indigestion, eased by taking the dose with food and avoiding rich or spicy meals, with a stomach-protecting medicine considered if it persists; thin skin, bruising, acne
Sweating; mood changes including irritability, anxiety or feeling low or high, which a minority of people experience and which are reported to a doctor
serious: Adrenal suppression: after more than 3 weeks the dose must be tapered, and extra cover is needed for illness and surgery; abrupt stopping can cause an adrenal crisis. Severe sickness, dizziness or extreme tiredness can signal adrenal problems, and a rounded 'moon' face with weight gain on the upper body signals Cushing's syndrome from prolonged excess
Osteoporosis and fractures (bone protection with bisphosphonates for long courses), avascular necrosis of the hip

Infections (masked and more severe: chickenpox, shingles, measles, TB reactivation), peptic ulcer with NSAIDs, cataract and glaucoma: a high temperature, a very sore throat, cough, pain on passing urine or a wound that will not heal can be signs of infection, and eyesight changes are reported
Psychosis, severe mood disturbance including depression, feeling high or thoughts of self-harm, which the NHS advises reporting to a doctor or NHS 111; growth suppression in children; muscle wasting

High blood sugar (excessive thirst, passing urine often, fruity-smelling breath), low potassium (muscle pain, cramps, changes in heart rate), inflamed pancreas (severe stomach or back pain), breathlessness or swelling of the arms or legs, unusual bruising or bleeding, red or black stools
Serious allergic reaction with swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue or difficulty breathing, which needs an emergency (999) call

cautions: Carry a steroid emergency card on courses longer than 3-4 weeks; the NHS issues a blue steroid card for courses of more than 3 weeks or at high doses
Never stop long-term steroids suddenly; sick-day doubling rules. Withdrawal causes tiredness, weakness, body aches and joint pain and the original condition can flare

Check for TB, hepatitis, diabetes and blood pressure before long courses; consider PPI and bone protection; people with diabetes may need their diabetes treatment adjusted by their clinician while on steroids
Live vaccines avoided on high doses; report exposure to chickenpox, shingles or measles if not immune
Real liquorice is avoided because it is thought to increase the amount of prednisolone in the body and the risk of low potassium
Taken once in the morning with food; the lowest dose that controls the condition is used, and long courses are reviewed for the lowest effective dose
prednisolone.monitoring: Blood pressure, glucose, weight; bone density and eye checks on long courses. The NHS lists the warning signs people are asked to watch for between reviews (signs of infection, of high blood sugar, of adrenal or Cushing's problems, mood change and eyesight change), and on long courses clinicians look for the slow harms of thinner bones, poorly controlled diabetes, high blood pressure and, in children, slowed growth.

sections.heading: What is prednisolone used for?
sections.body:
Prednisolone is a steroid, or corticosteroid, medicine. The NHS describes it as treating swelling (inflammation) and calming down the immune system. It is available only on prescription, as tablets or as a liquid that is swallowed.

The NHS lists conditions that may affect whether prednisolone is suitable, including recent infections, liver problems, heart failure, high blood pressure, diabetes, epilepsy and glaucoma. Steroids can also slow growth in children and teenagers.

sections.heading: How is prednisolone taken?
sections.body: The NHS says most people take prednisolone in the morning, because this stops it keeping them awake. Most people take it after breakfast. The NHS advises swallowing tablets whole with water and measuring the liquid with the cup or spoon supplied.

sections.heading: What are the side effects of prednisolone?
sections.body:
The NHS lists problems sleeping, weight gain and indigestion as the most common side effects. Headaches, feeling sick and mood changes such as irritability are also listed. Long-term use can lead to thinner bones (osteoporosis), poorly controlled diabetes, eyesight problems and slower growth in children and teenagers. Prednisolone can also make infections more likely.

Serious side effects are uncommon and are more likely with a high dose or longer use. They include a serious allergic reaction (anaphylaxis), mood changes including suicidal thoughts or mania, Cushing's syndrome, adrenal insufficiency. The NHS says to call 999 for possible anaphylaxis.

For signs of infection (such as a high temperature, a very sore throat, a cough or pain when peeing), high blood sugar, Cushing's syndrome, adrenal problems or low potassium, the NHS says to call a doctor or NHS 111 straight away. It says to talk to a doctor or contact NHS 111 about mood changes such as feeling depressed, feeling high or having strange and frightening thoughts, and to contact NHS 111 about thoughts of harming oneself. According to the NHS, black or dark brown vomit, or vomiting blood, means going to A&E.

sections.heading: Steroid treatment cards and stopping prednisolone suddenly
sections.body:
The NHS says people who take prednisolone for a longer period, or at a high dose, are given a blue steroid treatment card. A red steroid emergency card may also be recommended, depending on the risk to the adrenal glands, which a doctor or pharmacist assesses.

The NHS says prednisolone should not be stopped suddenly after long use or at high doses, because this can cause withdrawal side effects. Adrenal insufficiency is also among the serious side effects the NHS lists. For signs of adrenal problems, such as severe vomiting, dizziness, muscle weakness or weight loss, the NHS says to call a doctor or NHS 111 straight away. Sick day guidance from one NHS trust for people on long-term steroids says that vomiting with tablets that cannot be kept down needs a 999 call immediately.

sections.heading: Chickenpox, shingles and measles while taking prednisolone
sections.body: The NHS says to tell a doctor promptly after contact with someone who has an infectious illness such as measles, chickenpox or shingles while taking prednisolone. The NHS pages say to contact the doctor, or to see a pharmacist or call NHS 111, after such contact. The doctor may be able to prescribe a medicine to protect the person.

sections.heading: Other medicines, alcohol, liquorice and pregnancy
sections.body:
The NHS prednisolone page says alcohol can be drunk, though some NHS hospital leaflets note that it may irritate the stomach. The NHS says not to eat real liquorice while taking prednisolone.

The NHS pregnancy page says prednisolone can be taken during pregnancy. The NHS says the benefits usually outweigh any risks, and the baby's growth is checked regularly. For breastfeeding, the NHS says prednisolone can be taken if the doctor or health visitor confirms the baby is healthy. It passes into breast milk in small amounts and has been used for many years in breastfeeding women without side effects in their babies.

faqs.q: Can prednisolone be stopped suddenly?
faqs.a: The NHS says prednisolone should not be stopped suddenly after long use or at high doses, because this can cause withdrawal side effects. Adrenal insufficiency is among the serious side effects the NHS lists. For signs of adrenal problems, the NHS says to call a doctor or NHS 111 straight away.

faqs.q: Why do some people carry a steroid card?
faqs.a: People who take prednisolone for a longer period or at a high dose are given a blue steroid treatment card. A red steroid emergency card may be recommended, depending on the risk to the adrenal glands, which a doctor or pharmacist assesses.

faqs.q: What should happen after contact with chickenpox, shingles or measles?
faqs.a: The NHS says to tell a doctor promptly after contact with measles, chickenpox or shingles while taking prednisolone, and to contact the doctor, or see a pharmacist or call NHS 111.

faqs.q: Can a person drink alcohol or eat liquorice on prednisolone?
faqs.a: The NHS prednisolone page says alcohol can be drunk, though some NHS hospital leaflets note that it may irritate the stomach. The NHS says not to eat real liquorice.

faqs.q: When do prednisolone side effects need urgent help?
faqs.a: The NHS says to call a doctor or NHS 111 straight away for signs of infection, high blood sugar, Cushing's syndrome, adrenal problems or low potassium. Possible anaphylaxis needs a 999 call, and vomiting blood or black vomit means going to A&E. For thoughts of harming oneself, the NHS says to contact NHS 111.

allopurinol.name: Allopurinol
allopurinol.summary: A xanthine oxidase inhibitor that lowers uric acid in the blood, taken every day to prevent gout attacks and kidney stones rather than to treat an acute attack. It takes weeks to months to show its benefit, attacks can briefly become more frequent after starting, and once established it is considered safe to take for many years.
usedFor: Preventing gout attacks by lowering blood uric acid (started after the first attack settles, especially with repeated attacks, tophi, kidney stones or kidney disease)
Preventing uric acid kidney stones, including recurrent stones in people whose urine carries a lot of uric acid

Preventing tumour lysis syndrome during chemotherapy: some cancer treatments release large amounts of uric acid as cells break down, so allopurinol is started before the treatment begins; an intravenous form exists for people who cannot swallow tablets
allopurinol.howItWorks: Blocks xanthine oxidase, the enzyme that converts hypoxanthine and xanthine into uric acid at the end of purine breakdown. Blood urate falls below its saturation point, so no new crystals form and existing deposits in joints and tophi slowly dissolve over months. The dose is increased every few weeks until the urate target (below 360, or 300 micromol/L with tophi) is reached. The NHS explains the consequence for the reader: uric acid that cannot stay dissolved forms crystals, in joints (causing the swollen, painful attacks of gout) and in the kidneys (causing damage and stones), and allopurinol works by reducing the amount of uric acid the body's cells make, so that these crystals stop building up. Because existing crystals take time to dissolve, it may take several weeks for the uric acid level to fall and months for the full benefit to appear, and during that time attacks can paradoxically become more frequent; this is why it is started at a low dose, increased gradually, and usually covered with another medicine in the early months. It prevents attacks but does nothing to relieve an attack that has already started.
allopurinol.onset: Urate falls within days, but attacks can increase for the first 3-6 months as crystals dissolve, so colchicine or an NSAID is given as cover. The NHS notes that it may take several weeks for the uric acid level to fall far enough, and US information that the full benefit can take months; the medicine is continued even when the person feels well.

common: Rash or other skin reaction: the NHS advises stopping allopurinol and contacting a doctor straight away, because a rash can be the first sign of a serious skin reaction
Feeling sick, being sick, diarrhoea
Drowsiness, dizziness, sleepiness or problems with coordination, so driving is avoided until they pass
Gout flares in the first months of treatment
serious: Allopurinol hypersensitivity syndrome: severe skin reactions (Stevens-Johnson, toxic epidermal necrolysis) with liver and kidney involvement, rare but life-threatening, more likely in those with the HLA-B*58:01 gene (common in Han Chinese, Thai and Korean populations, who are screened), kidney disease and high starting doses; blistering or peeling skin is the warning sign
Severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) with swelling of the throat or tongue or difficulty breathing
Bone marrow suppression (a serious fall in white blood cells, which may show as unusual bruising with a high temperature or repeated infections), liver injury (rare)

cautions: Do not start during an acute attack; do not stop during an attack once established. Stopping allopurinol lets uric acid rise again and gout attacks may return, so it is not stopped without talking to the prescriber; a rash or other signs of a serious reaction need urgent medical advice
Interactions: azathioprine and mercaptopurine (levels rise dangerously), warfarin, ACE inhibitors and thiazides (hypersensitivity risk)
Drink plenty of fluid; reduce dose in kidney impairment. People with kidney or liver disease are started on a lower dose and monitored more closely
Started at a low dose and increased gradually, because raising the dose too quickly increases the risk of serious skin reactions
Febuxostat is the alternative if allopurinol is not tolerated, with cardiovascular caution
allopurinol.monitoring: Serum urate every 4 weeks during titration, then yearly; kidney and liver function. The NHS describes regular blood tests to check the uric acid level and closer monitoring for people with kidney or liver disease; new rashes are reported immediately rather than watched. Long-term treatment is regarded as very safe, so monitoring is about confirming the urate target and kidney function rather than screening for cumulative toxicity.

alendronate.name: Alendronate
alendronate.summary: A weekly bisphosphonate that slows bone breakdown, strengthening bone in osteoporosis and cutting the risk of hip and spine fractures. Its benefit builds slowly over months and treatment usually continues for some years, and the way the tablet is taken matters as much as the dose, because a tablet that lingers in the gullet can injure its lining.
usedFor: Osteoporosis: preventing hip, spine and wrist fractures in postmenopausal women and men at high risk
Bone protection during long courses of steroid tablets
Paget disease of bone, a disorder of over-active bone remodelling, which US patient information lists alongside osteoporosis as a use of oral alendronate
Zoledronic acid infusions for osteoporosis (yearly), Paget disease, bone metastases and high calcium in cancer
alendronate.howItWorks: The drug binds tightly to bone mineral, and when osteoclasts (the cells that dissolve bone) resorb that surface they take it up, which disables their metabolism and triggers their death. Resorption falls while bone-building osteoblasts keep working for a time, so bone density rises by a few per cent and, more importantly, the microarchitecture is preserved; hip fractures fall by about 40% and spine fractures by half. NHS information puts the same idea simply: alendronic acid slows the rate at which bone is broken down. Because bone remodels slowly, the effect is not immediate: bone mineral density begins to rise in the months after starting, and the medicine is usually continued for several years to gain the full effect. US patient information (MedlinePlus) describes the action as preventing bone breakdown and increasing bone density. The tablet is irritant to the lining of the oesophagus, which is why it is swallowed first thing in the morning with plain tap water before any food, drink or other medicine, and why staying upright afterwards protects the gullet; taken incorrectly it can cause ulcers of the food pipe or sores in the mouth.
alendronate.onset: Bone turnover falls within weeks; fracture reduction from about a year. NHS information notes that bone mineral density usually starts to rise in the months after starting and that several years of treatment are needed for the full effect. Usually 5 years, then reviewed (drug 'holiday').

common: Indigestion, heartburn, bloating or wind, abdominal pain, constipation or diarrhoea; staying upright for at least 30 minutes after a dose and eating smaller, more frequent meals ease the indigestion
Dizziness or a spinning sensation, headaches, feeling sleepy or tired
Muscle and joint aches, swollen joints, hands or legs; flu-like illness after the first zoledronic acid infusion
Severe or prolonged diarrhoea can stop the combined or progestogen-only contraceptive pill from working properly
serious: Oesophageal ulcers and strictures if the dosing instructions are not followed: new or worsening heartburn, or pain or difficulty on swallowing, are the warning signs and the NHS advises stopping the tablets and contacting a doctor or NHS 111
Osteonecrosis of the jaw (rare, mostly with high-dose cancer regimens; dental check before starting): a loose tooth, mouth sores, or jaw swelling or pain need review by both doctor and dentist
Atypical femoral fractures after many years of use: thigh, hip or groin pain is a warning that can precede a break in the thigh bone
Bleeding from the gut, showing as black or red stools
Eye inflammation with blurred vision or painful, red eyes
Low blood calcium, felt as muscle cramps or tingling around the mouth or in the fingers; kidney impairment with intravenous forms
Serious allergic reaction with swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue or difficulty breathing, which needs an emergency (999) call

cautions: Correct vitamin D deficiency and ensure adequate calcium before starting
Not used with eGFR below 35, swallowing disorders, active oesophageal disease, or inability to sit upright

Taken first thing in the morning, before food, drink or other medicines, with plain tap water only: the NHS advises against mineral water, tea, coffee, juice or milk, and against lying down for 30 minutes afterwards, to protect absorption and the oesophagus
Dental review and good oral hygiene; tell the dentist
Alcohol in moderation is permitted, but heavy drinking weakens bone and raises fracture risk, undoing part of the benefit
Review at 5 years (3 for zoledronate): continue in those at highest risk
alendronate.monitoring: Bone density scan every 3-5 years; calcium and vitamin D; kidney function for intravenous forms. Alendronate does not need routine drug-level or frequent blood monitoring; instead the NHS asks people to report the warning symptoms of its rarer harms promptly (new heartburn or swallowing difficulty, jaw or tooth problems, thigh or groin pain, eye pain, cramps or tingling) and reviews whether to continue after some years of treatment.

losartan.name: Losartan
losartan.summary: An angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB) that relaxes blood vessels to lower blood pressure and protect the kidneys in diabetes, an alternative for people who cough on ACE inhibitors.
usedFor: High blood pressure, particularly when an ACE inhibitor causes cough
Protecting the kidneys in type 2 diabetes with protein in the urine
Heart failure (candesartan, valsartan and losartan are the ARBs used) when ACE inhibitors are not tolerated
Reducing stroke risk in hypertension with a thickened left ventricle
losartan.howItWorks: Blocks the AT1 receptor that angiotensin II uses to constrict arteries, release aldosterone from the adrenal glands and thicken heart and vessel walls. With the receptor occupied, arteries relax, pressure falls, and the heart and the kidney's filters are unloaded. Because the converting enzyme is untouched, bradykinin does not build up, so the dry cough of ACE inhibitors is rare.
losartan.onset: Blood pressure falls over the first week; full effect in 3-6 weeks.

common: Dizziness, especially on standing at first
Tiredness, headache
A small rise in potassium and creatinine
serious: Acute kidney injury when dehydrated, with NSAIDs, or with narrowed renal arteries
High potassium with potassium supplements, spironolactone or kidney disease
Angio-oedema (rare)
Harm to the fetus: stop before or as soon as pregnancy is known

cautions: Sick-day rules: pause during vomiting, diarrhoea or fever
Not combined with an ACE inhibitor
Avoid with NSAIDs and potassium supplements
Bilateral renal artery stenosis and pregnancy: do not use
losartan.monitoring: Kidney function and potassium before starting, 1-2 weeks after each dose change, then yearly; blood pressure.

losartan.understand: Losartan blocks the action of angiotensin II, a hormone that narrows blood vessels and makes the body hold on to salt and water. With the hormone blocked, vessels relax and blood pressure falls, and the heart and kidneys are put under less strain.
losartan.mechanismDetail: Losartan and its more potent active metabolite (EXP3174) are selective, competitive antagonists at the angiotensin II type 1 (AT1) receptor. Blockade prevents angiotensin II-mediated vasoconstriction, aldosterone secretion, sodium reabsorption, sympathetic activation and the trophic effects on cardiac and vascular tissue. Efferent arteriolar dilatation lowers intraglomerular pressure, which underlies the reduction in proteinuria and slowing of diabetic nephropathy but also the rise in creatinine when renal perfusion depends on angiotensin II (renal artery stenosis, dehydration, NSAIDs). Because ACE is not inhibited, bradykinin is not accumulated and cough and angioedema are much less frequent than with ACE inhibitors. Losartan also has a mild uricosuric effect not shared by other ARBs.

pathway.label: Vascular smooth muscle, adrenal cortex, kidney
Angiotensin II cannot constrict vessels or release aldosterone
Lower blood pressure and glomerular pressure

indications.note: Diabetic nephropathy in type 2 diabetes with proteinuria, as part of antihypertensive treatment
Chronic heart failure when ACE inhibitors are unsuitable, initiated under specialist supervision
Also to reduce stroke risk in hypertension with left ventricular hypertrophy, and diabetic nephropathy with raised creatinine and proteinuria

warnings.text: US labelling carries a boxed warning on fetal toxicity: drugs that act on the renin-angiotensin system can cause injury and death to the developing fetus, and losartan should be discontinued as soon as pregnancy is detected.

UK information states losartan is not recommended in pregnancy or when trying to conceive, because it can harm the baby, particularly in the second and third trimesters; a different blood-pressure medicine is used.

warnings.text: Losartan can reduce kidney function and raise potassium, particularly with dehydration, NSAIDs, potassium supplements, potassium-sparing diuretics or narrowed renal arteries; kidney function and potassium are checked before treatment and after dose changes.
Angioedema (swelling of the face, lips, tongue or throat) is a rare but serious reaction that needs emergency treatment; it is less common than with ACE inhibitors but still possible.

Sick-day guidance: when vomiting, diarrhoea or fever cause dehydration, UK information advises that losartan may need to be paused temporarily to protect the kidneys, restarting once eating and drinking normally.

Losartan modestly lowers serum urate (a uricosuric effect not shared by other ARBs).

sections.heading: What is losartan used for?
sections.body: Losartan is a medicine for high blood pressure, and it belongs to the group called angiotensin II receptor blockers. The NHS says it can also be used to treat heart failure and for kidney problems in people with diabetes, where it helps to protect the kidneys. It is available on prescription only.

sections.heading: How does losartan work and how is it taken?
sections.body:
Losartan blocks the effect of a hormone called angiotensin II, which narrows blood vessels. The NHS says that, like other medicines in this group, losartan relaxes and widens the blood vessels, which lowers blood pressure and makes it easier for the heart to pump blood around the body.

The NHS says losartan can be taken with or without food, and that it should not be stopped unless a doctor says so, even when a person feels well.

sections.heading: What are the side effects of losartan?
sections.body:
The NHS lists dizziness, tiredness, headache, tummy pain, feeling or being sick, and swelling of the legs, ankles or feet as common side effects. It says losartan can make people feel dizzy, especially when they first start taking it or after a bigger dose, and that anyone who feels dizzy should not drive, ride a bike, or use tools or machinery until they feel better.

Taking losartan for a long time can sometimes mean the kidneys do not work as well as they should, so the doctor checks kidney function with regular blood tests. The NHS says yellow skin or yellow whites of the eyes may be a sign of liver problems, and that this can be harder to see on brown or black skin. For this, the NHS says to call a doctor or NHS 111 straight away. It also lists feeling weak, an irregular heartbeat, pins and needles and muscle cramps as possible signs of changes in blood potassium, with the same advice to call a doctor or NHS 111 straight away.

sections.heading: What are the signs of a serious allergic reaction or swelling?
sections.body: A serious allergic reaction to losartan is rare. The NHS says to call 999 if the lips, mouth, throat or tongue suddenly swell, or if breathing becomes difficult, and not to drive to A&E. A raised, itchy rash can also be part of an allergic reaction. Sudden swelling of parts of the body is called angioedema, and the NHS lists a past episode of it as a reason losartan may not be suitable.

sections.heading: Can losartan be taken with other medicines, alcohol or potassium salt substitutes?
sections.body:
The NHS lists painkillers such as ibuprofen, naproxen and diclofenac among the medicines that do not mix well with losartan. It also lists other blood pressure medicines, diuretics, lithium and heparin. A pharmacist or doctor can be asked about any combination.

The NHS advises against potassium-rich salt substitutes such as LoSalt, because they may push the level of potassium in the blood too high when mixed with losartan. Alcohol can add to the blood pressure lowering effect of losartan and may bring on dizziness or light-headedness. The NHS advises limiting alcohol while taking it, because alcohol can increase the risk of side effects.

sections.heading: Who needs extra care with losartan, including in pregnancy and during illness?
sections.body:
The NHS says losartan is not recommended in pregnancy, because it can reduce the fluid around the baby, particularly in the second and third trimesters. It advises women who could become pregnant to use contraception while taking it and to plan any pregnancy with their doctor. For breastfeeding, the NHS says to talk to a doctor or pharmacist first.

The NHS says losartan may not be suitable for people with a history of angioedema or with liver problems. It also says vomiting or diarrhoea can cause dehydration, and that a doctor or pharmacist may recommend stopping losartan until the person is better.

faqs.q: What are the common side effects of losartan?
faqs.a: The common side effects the NHS lists for losartan are dizziness, tiredness, headache, tummy pain, feeling or being sick, and swelling of the legs, ankles or feet.

faqs.q: What should happen if the lips or tongue swell while taking losartan?
faqs.a: Sudden swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue is treated as an emergency. The NHS says to call 999, and not to drive to A&E oneself. Past angioedema, meaning earlier sudden swelling of this kind, is also a reason losartan may not be suitable for a person.

faqs.q: Can painkillers like ibuprofen be taken with losartan?
faqs.a: The NHS lists painkillers such as ibuprofen, naproxen and diclofenac among the medicines that do not mix well with losartan. It also lists other blood pressure medicines among those that can interact.

faqs.q: Does alcohol affect losartan?
faqs.a: Alcohol can add to the blood pressure lowering effect of losartan. That may lead to dizziness or light-headedness. During the first few days of taking it, or after a bigger dose, the NHS says it is best to avoid alcohol until it is clear how the medicine affects the person.

lisinopril.name: Lisinopril
lisinopril.summary: An ACE inhibitor that lowers blood pressure, protects the heart after a heart attack and in heart failure, and slows kidney damage in diabetes by stopping the body making angiotensin II; taken once daily, with kidney function and potassium checked at the start.

lisinopril.howItWorks: Blocks angiotensin-converting enzyme, the enzyme in the lungs and blood vessels that turns inactive angiotensin I into angiotensin II. Less angiotensin II means arteries relax, the adrenal glands release less aldosterone so the kidneys keep less salt and water, and the pressure inside the kidney's filters falls. The same enzyme normally breaks down bradykinin, so bradykinin builds up: that adds to the vessel relaxation but also causes the dry cough in about one in ten people. Unlike most ACE inhibitors lisinopril is not a prodrug and is not metabolised by the liver.
lisinopril.onset: Blood pressure falls within hours of the first dose (which can cause first-dose hypotension); full effect after 2-4 weeks at a steady dose.

lisinopril.understand: Lisinopril stops your body making angiotensin II, a hormone that tightens blood vessels and makes the kidneys hold on to salt and water. Without it, vessels relax and the heart pumps against less resistance, so blood pressure falls and a weak heart has an easier job.
lisinopril.mechanismDetail: Lisinopril is a lysine analogue of enalaprilat that inhibits angiotensin-converting enzyme (kininase II) directly without needing hepatic activation. Reduced angiotensin II lowers arteriolar tone, aldosterone secretion, sodium retention and sympathetic drive, and dilates the efferent glomerular arteriole, lowering intraglomerular pressure and proteinuria. Accumulation of bradykinin contributes to vasodilation and to cough and angioedema. In heart failure the fall in afterload and preload and the interruption of neurohormonal activation improve symptoms and survival; after myocardial infarction, early treatment limits ventricular remodelling. Lisinopril is excreted unchanged by the kidney, so exposure rises as eGFR falls and doses are reduced accordingly.

sections.heading: What is lisinopril used for?
sections.body:
Lisinopril is an ACE inhibitor. The NHS says it is used to treat high blood pressure, a recent heart attack and kidney problems caused by diabetes, and it is also used with other medicines for heart failure. The NHS says most adults and children aged 6 years and over can take it.

For high blood pressure, heart failure and kidney disease caused by diabetes, treatment is usually long term and can continue for the rest of a person's life. The NHS says stopping lisinopril may cause blood pressure to rise, so it advises speaking to a doctor before stopping.

sections.heading: How does lisinopril work and how is it taken?
sections.body:
Lisinopril widens the blood vessels, which lowers blood pressure. The NHS says blood pressure can start to fall within hours, but the full effect may take a few weeks. In heart failure, improvement can take weeks or even months, and a lack of obvious change does not mean the medicine is not working.

The NHS says the tablets are swallowed whole with a drink of water, with or without food, and suggests taking them at the same time each day. The amount usually starts low and is increased gradually, and a doctor may suggest taking the first one before bedtime because it can cause dizziness.

sections.heading: What are the side effects of lisinopril?
sections.body:
The NHS lists these common side effects: headaches, feeling or being sick, diarrhoea, dizziness (especially on standing up quickly) and a dry cough that does not go away. Kidney problems are also listed as common, and blood tests can check for them. Dizziness is most likely when starting lisinopril or moving to a higher dose. The cough may take up to a month to clear after the medicine is stopped.

If a side effect such as the cough makes lisinopril hard to take, the NHS says a different type of blood pressure medicine may be possible. Because stopping may cause blood pressure to rise, it advises speaking to a doctor first.

Serious side effects are rare. The NHS says sudden swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue, or struggling to breathe, can be signs of a serious allergic reaction, and it says to call 999 for these. It also lists yellowing of the skin or the whites of the eyes, which can point to liver problems and may be harder to see on brown or black skin, and swollen ankles, blood in the pee or passing very little pee, which can point to kidney problems. For these, the NHS advises contacting a doctor or NHS 111.

sections.heading: Can lisinopril be taken with other medicines, alcohol or salt substitutes?
sections.body:
The NHS says alcohol can make the blood-pressure-lowering effect stronger and cause dizziness or light-headedness. It advises avoiding alcohol during the first few days of treatment or after an increase, until it is clear how the medicine affects a person.

The NHS says not to use salt substitutes such as Lo-Salt, because they are high in potassium and may push the potassium level in the blood too high. Its list of medicines to be careful with also includes other medicines that raise potassium, such as spironolactone, triamterene, amiloride, potassium supplements, trimethoprim and heparin. The list also includes anti-inflammatory painkillers such as ibuprofen, indomethacin and aspirin; the NHS says low-dose aspirin can be taken with lisinopril.

The NHS says to contact a doctor if there is a high temperature, sweats, shaking, or severe diarrhoea or vomiting. The doctor may tell the person to pause lisinopril until they recover.

sections.heading: Who needs extra care with lisinopril, and what about pregnancy and breastfeeding?
sections.body:
The NHS lists groups who may not be able to take lisinopril, including people who have had an allergic reaction to it or another medicine. It also lists people with heart, liver or kidney problems, diabetes, unstable or low blood pressure, and those having dialysis.

The NHS says lisinopril is not recommended in pregnancy. Its main concern is the baby's kidneys and lungs, particularly if it is taken in the second and third trimesters, and it says lisinopril should be stopped by 12 weeks of pregnancy at the latest. If someone is already pregnant, the NHS advises talking to a doctor as soon as possible, and says a different medicine can usually be prescribed.

For breastfeeding, the NHS says it might be OK to take lisinopril but to talk to a doctor or pharmacist first. The UK manufacturer leaflet is more cautious and says lisinopril is not recommended for mothers who are breastfeeding, and that a doctor may choose another treatment.

faqs.q: Does lisinopril cause a cough, and does it go away?
faqs.a: A dry cough that does not go away is one of the common side effects of lisinopril. The NHS says cough medicines do not usually help and that it can take up to a month to clear after the medicine is stopped. If the cough prevents someone taking lisinopril, a different type of blood pressure medicine may be possible, but the NHS advises speaking to a doctor before stopping because blood pressure may rise.

faqs.q: What are the signs of a serious allergic reaction or angioedema?
faqs.a: Angioedema is swelling of the lips, tongue and face. The NHS says sudden swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue, or struggling to breathe, can be signs of a serious allergic reaction, and it says to call 999. The NHS also says the chance of angioedema is higher for people with black skin.

faqs.q: Can salt substitutes or painkillers such as ibuprofen be used with lisinopril?
faqs.a: The NHS says not to use salt substitutes such as Lo-Salt, because they are high in potassium and may push the potassium level in the blood too high. It also lists anti-inflammatory painkillers such as ibuprofen, indomethacin and aspirin among medicines to be careful with, and says low-dose aspirin can be taken with lisinopril.

faqs.q: Can lisinopril be taken in pregnancy or while breastfeeding?
faqs.a: The NHS says lisinopril is not recommended in pregnancy, mainly because of effects on the baby's kidneys and lungs, and that it should be stopped by 12 weeks at the latest. It says a doctor can usually prescribe a different medicine. For breastfeeding, the NHS says it might be OK but to talk to a doctor or pharmacist first, while the UK manufacturer leaflet says it is not recommended for breastfeeding mothers.

rosuvastatin.summary: A high-intensity statin that lowers LDL cholesterol by more, milligram for milligram, than any other statin, used to prevent heart attacks and strokes when atorvastatin is not tolerated or not enough; the dose is limited by kidney function, ethnicity and interacting drugs.

rosuvastatin.howItWorks: Like atorvastatin it blocks HMG-CoA reductase, the enzyme that controls cholesterol production in the liver, so the liver takes more LDL out of the blood. Rosuvastatin is the most potent statin by weight (5-10 mg gives a similar LDL reduction to 20-40 mg of atorvastatin), is water-soluble, and is barely metabolised by the liver's CYP enzymes, so it has fewer interactions with antibiotics and antifungals; instead its levels depend on transporters and on the kidney, which is why doses are capped in kidney impairment, in people of Asian ancestry and with some HIV medicines; combining it with ciclosporin is contraindicated.

rosuvastatin.understand: Rosuvastatin blocks the enzyme the liver uses to make cholesterol, so the liver takes more LDL cholesterol out of your blood. Lower LDL means less build-up in artery walls and a lower risk of heart attack and stroke.
rosuvastatin.mechanismDetail: Rosuvastatin is a hydrophilic, hepatoselective HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor taken into hepatocytes by OATP1B1. It reduces cholesterol synthesis, upregulates LDL receptors and lowers LDL cholesterol by about 45-63% across the 5-40 mg range, with larger HDL increases than other statins. Only about 10% is metabolised (mainly CYP2C9, negligibly CYP3A4), so macrolides and azole antifungals have little effect; exposure is instead raised by OATP1B1 and BCRP inhibitors (ciclosporin, gemfibrozil, some protease inhibitors) and by reduced renal function, and is about twofold higher in people of Asian ancestry because of transporter polymorphisms, hence the dose caps. High doses can cause dose-related proteinuria of tubular origin.

azithromycin.name: Azithromycin
azithromycin.summary: A macrolide antibiotic that stops bacteria making proteins, given as a short course (often three days) for chest, ear, sinus, skin and sexually transmitted infections and as an alternative in penicillin allergy; long-lasting in tissues, with cautions about heart rhythm and interactions.
usedFor: Community-acquired pneumonia and other chest infections of mild to moderate severity (licensed use), including when atypical organisms (Mycoplasma, Chlamydia, Legionella) are suspected

azithromycin.howItWorks: Binds to the bacterial ribosome (the 50S subunit) and blocks the tunnel through which new proteins leave, so the bacterium cannot make the proteins it needs to grow. Human ribosomes are built differently and are not affected. Azithromycin is concentrated inside cells, particularly white cells, which carry it to sites of infection, and it lingers in tissues for days after the last dose, which is why courses are short. Because it barely interferes with the liver's drug-metabolising enzymes, it has fewer interactions than erythromycin and clarithromycin.
azithromycin.onset: Improvement expected within 2-3 days; tissue levels persist for 5-7 days after a 3-day course.

azithromycin.understand: Azithromycin stops bacteria from making the proteins they need to grow and multiply. Your immune system then clears the weakened bacteria. It builds up inside cells and stays in the body for days, so a course can be as short as three days.
azithromycin.mechanismDetail: Azithromycin is an azalide macrolide that binds reversibly to the 23S rRNA of the bacterial 50S ribosomal subunit within the peptide exit tunnel, blocking translocation and elongation of the nascent polypeptide; the effect is mainly bacteriostatic, bactericidal against some organisms at high concentrations. It achieves intracellular and tissue concentrations many times those in plasma, is delivered by phagocytes to infected tissue and has a tissue half-life of 2-4 days, allowing 3- to 5-day courses and single-dose regimens. Its spectrum includes streptococci, Haemophilus, Moraxella, atypical respiratory pathogens (Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydia, Legionella), Chlamydia trachomatis and Mycobacterium avium complex; pneumococcal macrolide resistance is common in some regions. Unlike erythromycin and clarithromycin it is a weak inhibitor of CYP3A4, but it inhibits P-glycoprotein (raising digoxin levels) and, like all macrolides, can prolong the QT interval. Long-term low-dose use in COPD and bronchiectasis works partly through anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory effects.

clopidogrel.name: Clopidogrel
clopidogrel.summary: An antiplatelet medicine that stops platelets clumping by blocking their P2Y12 receptor, taken to prevent clots after a heart attack, stent, stroke or in peripheral artery disease, often alongside aspirin for a defined period.
usedFor: Preventing further events after a heart attack or acute coronary syndrome, usually with aspirin for up to 12 months
After a coronary stent, to stop the stent clotting
After an ischaemic stroke or transient ischaemic attack, as long-term single antiplatelet treatment
Peripheral arterial disease
clopidogrel.howItWorks: Clopidogrel is a prodrug: the liver converts it, largely through the enzyme CYP2C19, into a molecule that binds irreversibly to the P2Y12 receptor on platelets. Without that receptor's signal, platelets cannot be activated by ADP and stick together far less readily. Because the block is permanent for the life of each platelet, the effect lasts about a week after stopping.
clopidogrel.onset: Antiplatelet effect within hours of a loading dose, or over several days at the usual daily dose; lasts 5-7 days after stopping as new platelets replace the blocked ones.

common: Bleeding more easily: nosebleeds, bruising, bleeding gums, longer bleeding from cuts

serious: Serious bleeding: blood in urine or stools, black stools, vomiting blood, a bleed after a head injury
Signs of an allergic reaction
Very rarely, a blood disorder causing fever, bruising and confusion (thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura)

cautions: Tell any doctor, dentist or pharmacist that you take it; it is usually paused before surgery only on the advice of the prescriber
Omeprazole and esomeprazole reduce its activation; other acid-suppressing medicines are preferred if one is needed
Combined with aspirin, warfarin, a DOAC or an NSAID the bleeding risk rises and the combination is decided by the prescriber
Some people convert it poorly (CYP2C19 variants) and get less protection
clopidogrel.monitoring: Signs of bleeding at every review; a full blood count if bleeding or bruising is unexplained. No routine level or test measures its effect.

bisoprolol.name: Bisoprolol
bisoprolol.summary: A once-daily beta blocker that selectively slows the heart and lowers its workload, used for heart failure, angina, high blood pressure and to control the rate in atrial fibrillation.
usedFor: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, where it improves survival
Angina
High blood pressure, usually when other classes are unsuitable or as an add-on
Rate control in atrial fibrillation and other fast rhythms
bisoprolol.howItWorks: Bisoprolol blocks beta-1 adrenoceptors on heart muscle and the conducting system, so adrenaline and noradrenaline can no longer speed the heart or make it contract as forcefully. The heart beats more slowly, needs less oxygen and, in heart failure, is protected from the long-term damage of sustained sympathetic drive. It has little effect on the beta-2 receptors of the airways at usual doses, though it is still used with caution in asthma.
bisoprolol.onset: Heart rate and blood pressure fall within hours; the benefit in heart failure builds over months. Not stopped suddenly: the dose is reduced gradually.

Never stopped abruptly: the dose is tapered

sections.heading: What is bisoprolol used for?
sections.body:
Bisoprolol is a beta blocker, a type of medicine used to treat high blood pressure and heart failure. It is also used to prevent the chest pain caused by angina, and to treat atrial fibrillation and other conditions that cause an irregular heartbeat. It is only available on prescription.

The NHS says bisoprolol works as well as other beta blockers at lowering blood pressure but is less likely to cause side effects, because it acts mainly on the heart. The British Heart Foundation (BHF) calls this kind of beta blocker selective, meaning it mostly blocks the effects of adrenaline and noradrenaline in the heart, with less effect on other parts of the body. Manufacturer leaflets say it is not recommended for children or adolescents.

sections.heading: How does bisoprolol work and how is it taken?
sections.body:
The BHF explains that beta blockers slow the heart rate and reduce how hard the heart has to work. They do this by blocking the effects of the stress hormones adrenaline and noradrenaline, which make the heart work harder and faster.

The NHS says bisoprolol tablets are swallowed with a drink of water and can be taken with or without food. It says treatment is usually long term, and that the very first dose can make some people feel dizzy. Doses differ between people and conditions, so none are given here. If someone feels dizzy or weak, the NHS advises stopping what they are doing and sitting or lying down until they feel better.

sections.heading: What are the side effects of bisoprolol?
sections.body:
The NHS lists headaches, tiredness, cold or tingly hands and feet, dizziness from low blood pressure, feeling or being sick, and diarrhoea or constipation as common side effects. They usually happen when treatment starts or when the amount is increased, and they often get better over time.

Serious side effects are uncommon. The NHS lists a serious allergic reaction, liver inflammation, breathing problems, and an irregular heartbeat or worsening heart failure symptoms. For a serious allergic reaction, the NHS says to call 999 if the lips, mouth, throat or tongue suddenly swell, or if breathing is very fast or hard. It says to call a doctor or NHS 111 if the whites of the eyes or the skin turn yellow, which can be a sign of liver problems.

sections.heading: Is it dangerous to stop bisoprolol suddenly?
sections.body:
The NHS says people still get the benefits of bisoprolol when they feel well. It advises talking to a doctor if you want to stop, because stopping can make blood pressure rise, which raises the risk of heart attack and stroke.

Manufacturer leaflets say that if bisoprolol is suddenly stopped, side effects are likely, and that treatment should not be stopped abruptly. Leaflets describe the amount being reduced gradually, and they say to speak to the prescriber before stopping.

sections.heading: Taking bisoprolol with other medicines or alcohol
sections.body:
The NHS says some medicines can interact with bisoprolol. Other medicines that lower blood pressure can sometimes push it too low, which may cause dizziness or fainting. Painkillers such as ibuprofen can make bisoprolol less effective. The NHS page also flags some decongestants and cold remedies, and medicines for asthma, COPD and diabetes. It says its list is not complete.

For herbal remedies and supplements the NHS says there is very little information, and it advises telling a doctor or pharmacist about any other medicines, herbal remedies, vitamins or supplements.

On alcohol, the NHS says it is best to avoid drinking when first starting bisoprolol or when the amount is increased, until you see how the medicine affects you. It also says alcohol will make dizziness or weakness feel worse.

sections.heading: Who needs extra care with bisoprolol?
sections.body:
The NHS says most adults aged 18 and over can take bisoprolol, but it is not suitable for everyone. It lists a previous allergic reaction to bisoprolol or another medicine, low blood pressure, a slow heart rate, worsening heart failure, heart disease, a recent heart attack, severe circulation problems, metabolic acidosis, and lung disease or severe asthma among the reasons to check with a doctor first. Manufacturer leaflets also list severe asthma and an untreated tumour of the adrenal gland called phaeochromocytoma as reasons not to take it. Bisoprolol may make the warning signs of low blood sugar harder to recognise.

The NHS says bisoprolol can be taken during pregnancy, but the mother and baby may be offered extra checks. Its pregnancy page says it can sometimes affect a baby's growth, so extra ultrasound scans may be needed. Taking it while breastfeeding may cause side effects in the baby, although a doctor may still recommend it if the benefits outweigh the risks. One UK product leaflet advises against use in pregnancy, which differs from the NHS advice.

faqs.q: Does bisoprolol make you tired?
faqs.a: The NHS lists tiredness as a common side effect of bisoprolol. Common side effects usually happen when treatment starts or the amount is increased, and they often get better over time. If someone feels dizzy or weak, the NHS advice is to stop what they are doing and sit or lie down until they feel better.

faqs.q: Can I stop taking bisoprolol if I feel fine?
faqs.a: The NHS says people still get the benefits of bisoprolol when they feel well, and that stopping can make blood pressure rise, raising the risk of heart attack and stroke. Leaflets say stopping suddenly is likely to cause side effects and that the amount is reduced gradually. The NHS advises talking to a doctor before stopping.

faqs.q: Does bisoprolol cause breathing problems?
faqs.a: The NHS lists breathing problems among the serious side effects of bisoprolol, which are uncommon. It says to call 999 if the lips, mouth, throat or tongue suddenly swell, or if breathing is very fast or hard. The NHS also lists lung disease or severe asthma among the conditions to check with a doctor before taking it.

faqs.q: Can I drink alcohol while taking bisoprolol?
faqs.a: The NHS says it is best to avoid alcohol when first starting bisoprolol or when the amount is increased, until you see how it affects you. It also says alcohol will make dizziness or weakness feel worse.

faqs.q: Is bisoprolol the same as other beta blockers?
faqs.a: Bisoprolol is one of several beta blockers. The NHS says it works as well as others for lowering blood pressure but is less likely to cause side effects because it acts mainly on the heart. The BHF says selective beta blockers mostly block adrenaline and noradrenaline in the heart, while non-selective ones also block them in other parts of the body.
